units.title: Sacraments: encounters with Christ
units.eq: How does Jesus meet us today?

lessons.title: Christ in the sacraments
lessons.idea: In the sacraments Jesus himself acts. Each is an outward sign that gives the grace it signifies, like the touch that healed the paralyzed man in Luke 5. The Church is the sacrament of Christ’s presence in the world.
lessons.question: What is a sign? What does it do?
lessons.activity: “Matter and form” lab (30 min). For Baptism (water; “I baptize you…”), Eucharist (bread and wine; words of consecration), Anointing (oil; the prayer), children match matter, form and minister on cards. Then explain why both are needed: the sign and the word.
teach: “What was visible in our Savior has passed over into his mysteries” (St Leo; CCC 1115). Jesus healed by touch, and now acts through the sacraments (CCC 1116).
A sacrament is an efficacious sign: it brings about what it signifies (CCC 1084, 1127). It has matter (the thing), form (the words) and a minister (CCC 1131).
The sacraments work by Christ’s own power, not the minister’s holiness (CCC 1128), but they bear fruit according to the faith of the receiver (CCC 1128).
Say plainly that grace is God’s life in us, a gift we cannot earn (CCC 1996–1999).
talk: What is the difference between a sign and a sacrament?
Which sacrament uses oil? Which uses bread and wine?
How do the sacraments help in daily life?
quiz: A sacrament…|Is a sign that gives grace|Is a ritual to impress|Is a school|Is only a symbol|0|CCC 1131.
“Matter and form” refer to…|The date and time|The sign and the words|The priest and server|The church and altar|1|CCC 1084.
Who instituted the sacraments?|The Pope|The apostles alone|The saints|Christ|3|CCC 1114.
lessons.life: Look for the matter of a sacrament in your parish (water, oil, bread, wine) and learn its words.
lessons.saint: Leo the Great: the pope who said that what was visible in Christ has passed into the sacraments.
misc: “I get grace by just being present.”
lessons.mem: “Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven.” (Matthew 9:2)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 5:17–26 up to the roof being opened. Ask, “What would you do for a friend?” Then finish the story and ask what Jesus did: he spoke and touched. He still does.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain for one sacrament its matter, form and minister.

script.open: Read Luke 5:17-26 aloud, or tell it, while two children act: friends lower a man through a roof to Jesus. Stop at the moment Jesus speaks. Ask, “Why did he forgive the man’s sins first, and heal his legs second? What was he showing?”
teach: Say: “Jesus did not only teach. He touched. He put mud on a blind man’s eyes. He took a girl by the hand. A woman touched his cloak and was healed. Jesus’ body was the way God’s love reached people. After Jesus rose and ascended, he did not stop touching us. He does it through the Church’s sacraments. Pope St. Leo said that what was visible in Christ passed into the sacraments.”

Say: “A sacrament is an outward sign, instituted by Christ, that gives the grace it signifies. There are always two parts, the sign and the words. The sign is called the matter, such as water, bread, wine or oil. The words are called the form, such as ‘I baptize you…’ and ‘This is my body.’ When a validly ordained minister celebrates the sacrament with the proper matter and form, and the right intention to do what the Church does, Christ himself acts.”

Say: “That is why the sacraments work no matter how holy or unholy the minister is: the true minister is Christ. But the sacraments are not magic. We receive their fruits according to our faith and readiness. The Church herself is called the sacrament of Christ’s presence, because she is the visible sign through which he acts in the world.”
ask: What are the two parts of a sacrament? (The sign, or matter; the words, or form.)
Who is the real minister of every sacrament? (Christ.)
Why are the sacraments not magic? (We must receive them with faith and openness.)
practice: Set out cards: Baptism (water; “I baptize you…”), Eucharist (bread and wine; “This is my body…”), Confirmation (chrism; “Be sealed…”), Anointing (oil; “Through this holy anointing…”), Reconciliation (words of absolution), Orders (laying on of hands), Matrimony (consent).
In teams, match the sacrament to its matter and its form.
For each, add: how is Jesus acting? (He washes, feeds, strengthens, heals, forgives, sends, binds.)
Share and check against a Catechism summary.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, you still touch us through the sacraments. Thank you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Name one sacrament and what Jesus does in it.”

tryit: Match each sacrament to its matter and form.
lessons.saintStory:
Leo was born in Italy around the year 400 and became pope in 440. At that time Rome was in great danger from barbarian invaders. In 452, when Attila the Hun marched toward Rome, Leo went out to meet him, and Attila turned back. In 455 he also persuaded the Vandals not to burn the city.
Leo was also a great teacher. He wrote a letter, called the Tome, explaining that Jesus is one Person with two natures, divine and human. When it was read at the Council of Chalcedon in 451, the bishops said, “Peter has spoken through Leo.”
In one of his sermons he wrote that what was visible in our Redeemer has passed into the sacraments. That is the idea of this lesson: the Jesus who touched and healed people now acts in the sacraments.

lessons.title: Three groups of sacraments
lessons.idea: The seven sacraments fall into three groups that match three needs of life: initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist) gives life, healing (Reconciliation, Anointing) restores it, and service of communion (Holy Orders, Matrimony) builds the Church.
lessons.question: How does each group serve people?
lessons.activity: “Life map” flowchart (25 min). Students draw a life path (birth, growing, falling ill, falling into sin, committing to a vocation) and mark which sacrament meets each moment. Add the signs. Read Acts 2:38 to see how early Christians began.
teach: Sacraments of Christian initiation lay the foundations of life (CCC 1212). Penance and Anointing heal (CCC 1421). Holy Orders and Matrimony are ordered to others’ salvation (CCC 1534).
The three groups echo human life: birth, growth, nourishment, healing, mission. Christian life is a real life in Christ.
Baptism, Confirmation and Holy Orders can only be received once because they imprint a character (CCC 1121). The others can be repeated.
Point out that Matrimony and Orders are both sacraments at the service of communion, and that each is a path to holiness.
talk: What human need does each group meet?
Which do you look forward to?
quiz: Penance is a sacrament of…|Healing|Marriage|Service|Initiation|0|CCC 1421.
Holy Orders is a sacrament of…|Service|Healing|Birth|Initiation|0|CCC 1534.
Baptism is a sacrament of…|Healing|Initiation|Service|Vocation|1|CCC 1212.
lessons.life: Ask a parent which sacraments they received and when.
lessons.saint: Charles Borromeo: an archbishop who built seminaries and fed the plague-stricken.
misc: “You can repeat Baptism if you fall away.”
lessons.mem: “Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins.” (Acts 2:38)
lessons.hook: Ask, “What do people need to be born, to get well, to belong?” Write the answers, then map them to the sacraments.
lessons.assess: Give a life situation and ask students to name the group and the sacrament.

script.open: Draw a long line on the board marked with ages 0, 10, 20, 40, 70. Ask, “What big things happen in a human life?” Write the answers on the line: birth, growing up, getting hurt, getting sick, falling in love, working, getting old. Say, “Notice how many of these God has a sacrament for.”
teach: Say: “There are seven sacraments, and they fit the three great needs of life. First, we need life and growth. The sacraments of initiation give it: Baptism gives new life, Confirmation strengthens us, and the Eucharist feeds us. The Catechism says they lay the foundations of every Christian life. Peter said on Pentecost, ‘Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins.’ (Acts 2:38)”

Say: “Second, we need healing. We get sick, and we sin. The sacraments of healing are Reconciliation, which forgives our sins and reconciles us to God and the Church, and the Anointing of the Sick, which strengthens us in serious illness or old age. Third, we need to serve one another and build up the Church. The sacraments at the service of communion are Holy Orders, in which men are ordained as bishops, priests and deacons to serve God’s people, and Matrimony, in which a man and a woman give themselves to each other and to their children.”

Say: “Not everyone receives all seven. Baptism, Confirmation and the Eucharist are for everyone. Holy Orders and Matrimony are for a particular calling. Orders and Baptism and Confirmation can only be received once, because they mark the soul forever. The Eucharist and Reconciliation we can receive again and again. Each sacrament meets us just where we are.”
ask: What are the three groups of sacraments? (Initiation, healing, service of communion.)
Which sacraments can we receive only once? (Baptism, Confirmation, Holy Orders.)
Why do we need sacraments of healing? (We get sick and we sin.)
practice: Give each student a long sheet. Draw a winding life path from birth to old age.
Mark where each sacrament fits: birth (Baptism), growing up (Confirmation, Eucharist), when we fall (Reconciliation), when we are sick (Anointing), vocation (Orders or Matrimony).
Color-code the three groups.
Explain your life map to a partner.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, thank you for meeting us at every stage of life.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Explain the three groups of sacraments to someone.”

tryit: Draw a life path from birth to old age.
lessons.saintStory:
Charles Borromeo was born in 1538 into a noble family in northern Italy. When he was twenty-two, his uncle, who was pope, made him a cardinal, and Charles was not sure what that was for. After his older brother died, he decided to live as a priest should, and he took his responsibilities seriously.
In 1564 he became archbishop of Milan. He visited all the parishes in his large diocese, even in the high Alps. He started seminaries to train priests well, schools of Christian doctrine for children on Sundays, and carefully taught that the sacraments should be celebrated with reverence. In 1576, when the plague came to Milan, he stayed. He organized food, care for the sick and prayer, and walked barefoot in procession.
Charles died in 1584, at forty-six. He shows how the sacraments, in every stage of life, reach the whole people of God.

lessons.title: Signs and symbols
lessons.idea: The Church’s liturgy uses signs and symbols: water, oil, light, bread, wine, incense, gestures. They come from creation and the Bible, and are filled with new meaning by Christ.
lessons.question: What do these signs mean?
lessons.activity: “Symbol museum” (30 min). Display real objects and let students explain them to a partner: water (washing and new life), oil (strength and anointing), light (Christ), incense (prayer rising), bread/wine (Eucharist), hands (blessing), kneeling (adoration). Match each to a verse (Psalm 51:7; Psalm 141:2; John 8:12).
teach: In the liturgy, signs from creation, human life and the covenant are assumed by Christ (CCC 1145–1152). Water, oil, bread and wine each have deep biblical roots.
Gestures and postures speak: standing for respect and joy, kneeling for adoration, bowing for reverence, the Sign of the Cross for faith (CCC 1155–1162).
Images (icons, statues) honor persons, not material things (CCC 1159–1162). Sacred music and art lift our minds to God.
Teach that symbols are not decorations. Ask what each shows about God.
quiz: Oil signifies…|Cleaning|Cooking only|Rest|Strength and the Spirit|3|CCC 1293.
Light signifies…|Fire only|Christ|Noise|Electricity|1|CCC 1189.
The laying on of hands signifies…|Waving|Giving the Spirit|Fear|Greeting|1|CCC 1150.
lessons.life: Notice and name three signs at Mass this Sunday.
lessons.saint: Helena: the empress who sought the cross of Jesus and built churches.
misc: “Incense and candles are just for show.”
lessons.mem: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you.” (Psalm 141:2)
lessons.hook: Show a flag, a wedding ring, a handshake. “What do these say without words?” Then reveal a candle, a cup of water, a bottle of oil.
lessons.assess: Ask students to choose a symbol and explain what it means and where it appears in church.

script.open: Set out a mystery bag with objects: a candle, a small dish of water, a cross, a piece of bread, a bottle of oil, a stole, some incense. Pull them out one at a time. Ask, “What do you use this for? Where have you seen it?”
teach: Say: “The Church’s liturgy uses signs and symbols. A symbol is something visible that points to something invisible. God made us body and soul, so we learn about invisible things through visible ones. Many of the symbols come from creation: water, oil, fire, bread, wine, light. Others come from the Bible: the cross, the lamb, the dove. And Jesus has given them new meaning.”

Say: “Water: washes and gives life; at Baptism it shows that we are cleansed and reborn. Psalm 51:7: ‘Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.’ Oil: heals, strengthens and anoints; it is used for Baptism, Confirmation, Holy Orders and the Anointing of the Sick. Light: Christ is the light of the world; we light candles. Bread and wine: the food of life, they become the Body and Blood of Christ. Incense: our prayer rising to God. Psalm 141:2: ‘Let my prayer be counted as incense before you.’”

Say: “There are also signs we do with our bodies: kneeling shows adoration, standing shows respect and readiness, bowing shows reverence, the Sign of the Cross claims us for Christ, and the laying on of hands passes on a blessing or a mission. The signs speak when words are not enough. When we understand what they mean, we pray with our whole selves.”
ask: What is a symbol? (A visible sign that points to something invisible.)
What does water show in Baptism? (Cleansing and new life.)
What does incense show? (Our prayer rising to God.)
practice: Set up a “symbol museum” with real objects: water, oil, a candle, a cross, bread and wine (grape juice), incense (or a picture), a white garment, a stole.
Pairs visit each object. One explains what it is used for, what it means, and a Bible verse that goes with it. The other asks a question.
Switch partners.
Choose one and write a three-sentence label for the museum.
script.close: Pray Psalm 141:2: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look for three signs at Mass this Sunday.”

tryit: Explain one object to a partner.
Say what it shows about God.
lessons.saintStory:
Helena was born around the year 250, probably to a poor family in the Roman Empire. She married a Roman officer, and their son was Constantine, who became emperor. Constantine made Christianity legal and allowed Christians to worship in peace.
When Helena was about seventy-five, she traveled to the Holy Land as a pilgrim. She visited the places where Jesus lived, and she helped to build churches over the places of his birth in Bethlehem and his ascension on the Mount of Olives. According to tradition she also discovered the cross of Jesus in Jerusalem.
Helena shows how we use signs and holy places to remember Jesus. The cross is the greatest Christian symbol, and Helena’s love for it reminds us how much the signs of our faith matter.

lessons.title: Baptism
lessons.idea: Baptism is the gateway to the other sacraments. It forgives original sin and all personal sin, makes us children of God, and joins us to the Church. Its sign is water poured three times with the words “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”
lessons.question: What are the effects of Baptism?
lessons.activity: “Baptism step by step” (30 min). Lay out the rite on cards: sign of the cross, readings, anointing with the oil of catechumens, blessing of water, renunciation and profession of faith, pouring, chrism, white garment, candle. Students put them in order and say what each means. Read Romans 6:3–4.
teach: Baptism is “the basis of the whole Christian life, the gateway to life in the Spirit” (CCC 1213). It removes original and personal sin and brings new birth (CCC 1263–1264).
Romans 6:3–4: we are buried with Christ and raised to new life. The water has been a sign of death and life since the Flood and the Red Sea (CCC 1217–1222).
Ordinarily a bishop, priest or deacon baptizes, but in an emergency anyone can, with water and the words (CCC 1256). Infants are baptized because grace is a gift (CCC 1250–1252).
Baptism marks the soul forever (CCC 1272–1274). Adults who are not baptized prepare through the catechumenate (RCIA).
talk: What does the white garment signify?
What do you renounce at Baptism?
quiz: Baptism removes…|Original sin and personal sin|Shyness|Hunger|Nothing|0|CCC 1263.
Baptism imprints…|An indelible character|A bruise|A name only|A tattoo|0|CCC 1272.
The ordinary minister is…|A bishop, priest or deacon|Anyone|A teacher|A parent only|0|CCC 1256.
lessons.life: Renew your baptismal promises at Easter.
lessons.saint: Peter Claver: a priest who baptized hundreds of thousands of enslaved people and treated them as children of God.
misc: “Unbaptized babies cannot be saved” (the Church entrusts them to God’s mercy, CCC 1261).
lessons.mem: “Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” (John 3:5)
lessons.hook: Pour water into a bowl and ask, “What does water do?” (cleans, quenches, gives life, can drown). Say the Church uses all four meanings in Baptism.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the effects of Baptism and the roles of matter, form and minister.

script.open: Have a child pour water into a bowl while you ask, “What does water do? It can wash, it can quench thirst, it can drown, it can make things grow. In Baptism, God uses water to do something much greater.”
teach: Read Romans 6:3-4. Say: “Paul wrote: ‘Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, so that as Christ was raised from the dead, we too might walk in newness of life.’ Baptism joins us to Jesus’ death and Resurrection. We die to sin, and rise to a new life.”

Say: “Baptism is the gateway to all the sacraments. It forgives original sin and all personal sins, and also all punishment for sin. It makes us children of God, temples of the Holy Spirit, and members of the Church. It leaves a permanent spiritual mark, called a character, which is why we are baptized only once. The sign is water, poured over the head three times (or the person is immersed), with the words, ‘I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’”

Say: “In an emergency, anyone can baptize, using water and the Trinitarian words, with the intention of doing what the Church does. The rite includes the Sign of the Cross, readings, the prayer of exorcism (to free us from evil), the anointing with the oil of catechumens, the blessing of the water, the baptismal promises, the pouring of the water, the anointing with chrism, the white garment (a sign of new life), and a lighted candle from the Easter candle (Christ our light). Parents and godparents promise to help the child grow in faith.”
ask: What does Baptism do? (Forgives sin, makes us children of God, joins us to the Church.)
Who can baptize in an emergency? (Anyone, with water and the right words and intention.)
Why are we baptized only once? (It leaves a permanent mark on the soul.)
practice: Lay out cards with the steps of the Baptism rite: sign of the Cross, readings, anointing with oil of catechumens, blessing of the water, renunciation of sin and profession of faith, pouring of water, anointing with chrism, white garment, candle.
Students put them in order and write the meaning of each sign beside it.
Read the baptismal promises aloud, taking turns.
Everyone answers, “I do.”
script.close: Renew your baptismal promises together. Make the Sign of the Cross with water. Send home: “Ask when and where you were baptized, and who your godparents are.”

tryit: Put the steps of Baptism in order.
lessons.saintStory:
Peter Claver was born in 1580 in Spain, and joined the Jesuits. He was sent to the city of Cartagena, in what is now Colombia, which was a major port for the slave trade. Thousands of men, women and children were brought there on ships from Africa, in terrible conditions.
When a ship arrived, Peter went on board, even in the hold, with food, water, medicine and friends who could translate. He cared for the sick, and he taught the Christian faith and baptized them. He wanted them to know that they were beloved children of God, even though they were being treated as property. He is said to have baptized over 300,000 people in forty years. He signed his name, “Peter, slave of the slaves forever.”
He died in 1654. Peter Claver shows that Baptism makes every person a child of God, with dignity.

lessons.title: Confirmation
lessons.idea: Confirmation completes Baptism. The bishop (or a priest delegated) anoints the forehead with chrism and says “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.” We receive the seven gifts and are sent to witness.
lessons.question: What gifts do we receive?
lessons.activity: “Seven gifts” chart (25 min). Students make a card for each gift (wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord / wonder and awe), write a definition, and give an example for each. Read Acts 8:14–17. Then plan the next parish Confirmation prayer.
teach: Confirmation perfects baptismal grace and seals us with the Spirit (CCC 1285, 1302–1303). The sign is anointing with chrism by the laying on of hands and the words “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1300).
The seven gifts of the Spirit (Isaiah 11:2) strengthen us for witness (CCC 1830–1831). The fruits (love, joy, peace…) show them at work (CCC 1832).
The ordinary minister is the bishop, which shows our bond with the apostles; priests may confirm in some cases (CCC 1312–1313).
Confirmation is a beginning, not a graduation. Invite students to name how they will witness.
talk: How have you seen the fruits in someone?
quiz: The matter of Confirmation is…|Water|Ashes|Chrism|Bread|2|CCC 1297.
Confirmation seals us with…|A name|A medal|The Holy Spirit|A ring|2|CCC 1302.
One of the fruits of the Spirit is…|Wealth|Joy|Fame|Speed|1|Galatians 5:22.
lessons.life: Pray the Veni Sancte Spiritus or Come Holy Spirit daily.
lessons.saint: Pedro Calungsod: a teenage catechist who stayed with a priest to the end.
misc: “Confirmation means I confirm my faith, and it’s optional.”
“Confirmation is the end of religious ed.”
lessons.mem: Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love.
lessons.hook: Ask, “What was different about the apostles before and after Pentecost?” (hiding versus preaching). Confirmation gives the same Spirit for the same mission.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name all seven gifts and tell the sign and words of Confirmation.

script.open: Say, “Make a bold promise. For example, ‘I will always finish what I start.’ How hard is it to keep? In Confirmation, we receive help to live out our faith boldly.”
teach: Read Acts 8:14-17. Say: “When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the word of God, they sent Peter and John. They prayed that the new believers might receive the Holy Spirit, for the Spirit had not yet come upon them. Then Peter and John laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit. This is the beginning of the sacrament of Confirmation.”

Say: “Confirmation completes Baptism. The bishop, or a priest he delegates, anoints the forehead with chrism, a blessed oil mixed with perfume, and says, ‘Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.’ He also lays on hands. The oil means strengthening and sealing. We receive the Holy Spirit in a special way, and a permanent mark, so we can be confirmed only once. We are made stronger to live and share the faith, like soldiers of Christ.”

Say: “The Spirit gives us seven gifts: wisdom (seeing life as God sees it), understanding (grasping the truths of faith), counsel (choosing well), fortitude (courage), knowledge (knowing God through creation and Scripture), piety (loving reverence for God), and fear of the Lord (wonder and awe before God). The fruits of the Spirit are what grow from the gifts: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. The confirmed are sent out to witness to Christ by their words and actions.”
ask: What does the bishop say at Confirmation? (Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.)
Name three gifts of the Holy Spirit. (Wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord.)
Why does Confirmation matter? (It strengthens us to live and witness to the faith.)
practice: Make seven cards, one for each gift of the Spirit.
On each, write what the gift means in simple words and an example of using it (for instance, fortitude: standing up for someone who is bullied).
Choose the gift you most need right now, and write a short prayer asking for it.
Share one example with a partner.
script.close: Pray the prayer to the Holy Spirit: “Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask your parents about their Confirmation.”

tryit: Make a card for each gift of the Spirit.
Write what each gift helps you do.
lessons.saintStory:
Pedro Calungsod was born in the Philippines around 1654. As a teenager, he was trained by the Jesuits there as a catechist, which means a teacher of the faith. When he was about fourteen or fifteen, he joined a group of missionaries who sailed to the island of Guam, in the Pacific, to share the Gospel with the Chamorro people.
Pedro helped build churches, taught the faith, and baptized dying infants. He was strong and gentle and a skilled helper. Some people on the island did not welcome the missionaries, and in 1672 a group attacked Father Diego de San Vitores, who was baptizing a child. Pedro could have run away. Instead he stayed, and was killed with the priest.
He was about seventeen years old, and was named a saint in 2012. Pedro shows the courage that the Holy Spirit gives in Confirmation.

lessons.title: Living as the baptized
lessons.idea: By Baptism we share in Christ’s three roles: priest (offering our lives to God), prophet (witnessing to the truth) and king (serving others). Every baptized person has a mission.
lessons.question: How do you live your baptism?
lessons.activity: “Baptismal promise card” (25 min). Students write a personal card with three promises: one as priest (pray/offer a sacrifice this week), one as prophet (speak up for truth or a friend), one as king (serve someone). Read 1 Peter 2:9.
teach: Through Baptism we share in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and kingly office (CCC 897–913, 783–786). The ordained priesthood and the common priesthood differ in kind, not only in degree (CCC 1547).
Priest: offer our work, prayers, joys and sufferings with Christ (CCC 901, 1141). Prophet: witness to the faith in word and life (CCC 904–907). King: master ourselves and serve (CCC 908–913).
“You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9). The laity bring Christ into the world (CCC 898–900).
Link to the baptismal promises renewed at Easter.
talk: How do you serve as a priest, prophet and king?
quiz: The baptized share in Christ as…|Judge, jury, executioner|Priest, prophet and king|Teacher, lawyer, doctor|Soldier, farmer, merchant|1|CCC 897.
To be a prophet is to…|Hide|Witness to Christ|Predict lottery numbers|Lead armies|1|CCC 904.
Kingship means…|Buying|Hiding|Ruling harshly|Serving|3|CCC 908.
lessons.life: Do a small act of service in your parish.
lessons.saint: Frédéric Ozanam: a young layman who helped the poor and defended the faith.
lessons.mem: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation.” (1 Peter 2:9)
lessons.hook: Show a crown, a scroll and a chalice. “Who has all three?” (Jesus). Then say: we share in all three.
lessons.assess: Ask each student to give one example of acting as priest, prophet and king.

script.open: Ask, “Who has a job to do in the Church? Priests? The Pope? Anyone else?” Let children respond. Then say, “By Baptism, every one of us shares in Jesus’ own work. Let’s see how.”
teach: Read 1 Peter 2:9. Say: “‘You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own people, that you may declare the wonderful deeds of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.’ In Baptism, we are united to Christ, who is priest, prophet and king. And we share in his three roles.”

Say: “Priest: Jesus offered himself to the Father. We share in this by offering our lives to God: our prayers, work, joys and sufferings, especially at Mass. We are a priestly people, and we sanctify the world. Prophet: Jesus spoke God’s truth. We share in this by witnessing to the truth by our words and our example, in our families, school and work. King: Jesus served as a king who washed feet. We share in this by serving others, and by ruling ourselves, mastering our own sin.”

Say: “Some people have a special vocation as priests or religious. But all of us have a role. The laity are the Church’s presence in the world, in families, in business, in schools, in politics, in the arts. The Second Vatican Council taught that all Christians are called to holiness. Your Baptism is not a past event but a mission. Think about what yours is.”
ask: What three roles of Christ do we share? (Priest, prophet and king.)
How do we share in the priesthood of Christ? (Offering our lives to God, prayer and Mass.)
What is a way to be a prophet at school? (Tell the truth, defend someone, live by faith.)
practice: Fold a card in three parts: priest, prophet, king.
In each, write one specific promise. For example: Priest: “I will pray the Morning Offering every day.” Prophet: “I will not join in gossip.” King: “I will help with the dishes without being asked.”
Decorate the card with a cross and water drops (baptism).
Share one with a partner and ask for accountability.
script.close: Renew your baptismal promises. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Put your card where you will see it every day.”

tryit: Write three promises: one for priest, one for prophet, one for king.
lessons.saintStory:
Frédéric Ozanam was born in 1813 in Milan and grew up in Lyon, France. He was a bright student, and went to Paris to study at the Sorbonne. Many of his professors and fellow students said that the Church was out of date, and he found his faith shaken for a time. But he defended the faith with arguments and with kindness.
When some students challenged him by saying that the Church did nothing for the poor, he answered, “Let us go to the poor.” In 1833, at twenty, he and a few friends started a group that visited poor families, bringing food and firewood. They took the name of Saint Vincent de Paul. It became the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul, which now has members all over the world.
He was also a professor, a husband and a father. He died in 1853, at forty. Frédéric shows what a lay person can do: live as priest, prophet and king through ordinary work.

lessons.title: The source and summit
lessons.idea: The Eucharist is “the source and summit of the Christian life.” Every sacrament and work of the Church flows from it and leads to it, because in it we have Christ himself.
lessons.question: Why “source and summit”?
lessons.activity: “Source and summit” diagram (25 min). In a circle put the Eucharist, then draw arrows from and to it for each sacrament, the parish ministries, prayer, service. Read John 6:35 and discuss: “I am the bread of life.”
teach: “The Eucharist is the source and summit of the Christian life” (Lumen Gentium 11; CCC 1324). The other sacraments and ministries are bound up with it (CCC 1325).
It is called by many names: Thanksgiving, Lord’s Supper, Breaking of Bread, Holy Sacrifice, Holy Communion (CCC 1328–1332).
At the Last Supper Jesus instituted it “on the night he was betrayed” and commanded “Do this in memory of me” (Luke 22:19; CCC 1337–1340).
Use John 6:35 (“I am the bread of life”) to connect Scripture to the sacrament.
talk: Why is the Eucharist the center?
What other names do we use?
quiz: The Eucharist is the…|Surprise|Beginning only|Source and summit|Option|2|CCC 1324.
“Eucharist” means…|Thanksgiving|Party|Meal|Sacrifice|0|CCC 1328.
Another name is…|Game|Prayer|Holy Communion|Show|2|CCC 1331.
lessons.life: Offer a prayer of thanks after Communion.
lessons.saint: Peter Julian Eymard: a priest who spent his life spreading love for the Eucharist.
lessons.mem: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger.” (John 6:35)
lessons.hook: Draw a mountain with a stream starting near the top. “Where does the stream begin and where does it end?” The Eucharist is both the source and the goal.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain “source and summit” in their own words.

script.open: Draw a circle on the board and ask, “What is the center of a wheel? Without a center, nothing holds together. Is there a center in the Church’s life?”
teach: Read John 6:35. Say: “Jesus said, ‘I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.’ He said this after he fed five thousand people with five loaves and two fish. Then he said that the bread he would give is his flesh, for the life of the world. The Eucharist is the fulfillment of that promise.”

Say: “The Second Vatican Council called the Eucharist ‘the source and summit of the Christian life.’ Source means everything flows from it, like a spring. Summit means everything leads toward it, like the top of a mountain. All the other sacraments, all ministries and works of the Church are connected to it, and directed to it, because in the Eucharist we have Christ himself, our Pasch (Passover).”

Say: “Think of it this way. Baptism brings us to the table. Confirmation strengthens us for the journey. Reconciliation cleans us so we can receive worthily. The Anointing of the Sick prepares us for the final journey. Marriage and Holy Orders serve the family of the Church that gathers. And every Mass sends us out to love. When we celebrate the Eucharist, we unite ourselves to Christ’s sacrifice on the cross, and with the whole Church.”
ask: What does ‘source and summit’ mean? (Everything flows from it and leads to it.)
What did Jesus say about himself in John 6? (I am the bread of life.)
How are other sacraments connected to the Eucharist? (They prepare for, flow from or lead to it.)
practice: Draw a large circle with the Eucharist at the center.
Around it, put the other six sacraments. Draw arrows to or from each, and write how it relates to the Eucharist.
Add one arrow for “mission,” going out from the Eucharist into the world.
Explain your diagram to a partner.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, you are the bread of life. We believe in you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Spend five minutes before the tabernacle if you can.”

tryit: Draw the Eucharist in the middle.
Draw arrows from the other sacraments.
Explain why it is the source and summit.
lessons.saintStory:
Peter Julian Eymard was born in France in 1811. As a boy, he loved to stay in the church to pray in front of the tabernacle. He was so small that the sacristan sometimes found him on tiptoe to look at it.
He became a priest and joined the Marists, but he felt called to give his whole life to the Eucharist. In 1856 he started a new congregation, the Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament, whose members spend time each day adoring Jesus in the Eucharist and encouraging others to do the same. He also started a group for women, and a group of lay people to keep the Eucharistic fire alive.
He is called “the Apostle of the Eucharist.” He died in 1868. Peter Julian shows that the Eucharist is the center of Christian life.

lessons.title: The Real Presence
lessons.idea: In the Eucharist, bread and wine become the Body and Blood, Soul and Divinity of Jesus Christ. The Church calls this transubstantiation. Christ is really, truly and substantially present.
lessons.question: How do we know Jesus is truly present?
lessons.activity: “Witness file” (30 min). Teams review the evidence: Scripture (John 6; Luke 22:19–20; 1 Corinthians 11:23–29), the Fathers (Ignatius of Antioch, Justin Martyr, Cyril of Jerusalem) and the Church’s teaching (CCC 1373–1381). Each writes a one-paragraph “case.” Then gather around a tabernacle for a silent visit.
teach: Christ is present in the Church gathered, in the Word, in the priest and, above all, “in the Eucharistic species” (CCC 1373). This is real presence “in the fullest sense” (CCC 1374).
Transubstantiation: the substance of bread and wine become Christ’s Body and Blood, while the appearances remain (CCC 1376–1377). Trent (1551) defined this (CCC 1376).
Early Christians believed this. St Ignatius (c. 107) calls the Eucharist “the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ” (CCC 1374). Justin Martyr (c. 155) says the same.
Eucharistic adoration flows from this belief (CCC 1378–1381). Teach reverent behavior before the tabernacle.
quiz: Transubstantiation means…|Nothing changes|Bread symbolizes Christ|Christ is only remembered|The substance of bread and wine becomes Christ’s Body and Blood|3|CCC 1376.
The Real Presence includes…|Only memory|Body, blood, soul and divinity|Only the Body|Only a feeling|1|CCC 1374.
We kneel to…|Adore|Hide|Pray silently|Rest|0|CCC 1378.
lessons.life: Spend 10 minutes with Jesus in the tabernacle.
lessons.saint: Juliana of Liège: a nun who asked for a feast to honor the Body and Blood of Christ.
misc: “It changes only when we believe it.”
lessons.mem: “This is my body, which is given for you.” (Luke 22:19)
lessons.hook: Read John 6:51–58 slowly. Ask what Jesus says (“my flesh is true food”) and what the crowd did (many left). “He did not say, ‘I was only speaking in symbols.’ ”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what happens at consecration, using “substance” and “appearance.”

script.open: Show a loaf of bread. Say, “What is this? And after a priest says the words of consecration, what is it? If I told you that something looks and tastes like bread but is Jesus himself, how would you check?”
teach: Read John 6:51-58 in pieces. Say: “Jesus said, ‘I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.’ The people argued, ‘How can this man give us his flesh to eat?’ Jesus did not take it back. He said it again, even more strongly: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.’ Many left him. He did not call them back to say it was a symbol.”

Say: “At the Last Supper, Jesus took bread and said, ‘This is my body,’ and the cup, ‘This is my blood.’ (Luke 22:19-20) Paul wrote, ‘The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?’ (1 Corinthians 10:16) The early Fathers, such as Ignatius of Antioch and Justin Martyr, said the same: it is not common bread.”

Say: “The Church teaches that in the Eucharist, the whole Christ is present: Body, Blood, Soul and Divinity. This is called the Real Presence. The word transubstantiation means that the substance, what the thing really is, changes into Christ’s Body and Blood, while the appearances, or accidents, of bread and wine remain. This is a miracle, not an object of science. We believe because Christ said so, and the Church has always taught it. And we adore him in the Blessed Sacrament.”
ask: What does the Real Presence mean? (Jesus is truly, really and substantially present in the Eucharist.)
What is transubstantiation? (The substance of bread and wine changes into Christ’s Body and Blood; appearances remain.)
What do we do before the Blessed Sacrament? (Adore, genuflect, pray.)
practice: Set up a “witness file.” In teams, review evidence from Scripture (John 6:51-58, Luke 22:19-20, 1 Corinthians 11:23-29), the early Church (Ignatius and Justin), and the Church’s teaching.
Each team writes a one-paragraph summary: What does this witness say?
Teams present their evidence in a short “trial” where one student asks questions and others answer.
Write a one-sentence statement of the Church’s faith.
script.close: Pray the Adoro Te or: “Jesus, I adore you in the Blessed Sacrament.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Genuflect with reverence at Mass.”

tryit: Review the evidence for the Real Presence.
lessons.saintStory:
Juliana was born around 1193 near Liège, in what is now Belgium. She became an orphan when she was five and was raised by nuns. When she was sixteen, she began to have a vision of a bright moon with a dark spot. She came to understand that the moon was the Church’s year, and the dark spot was the absence of a feast in honor of the Blessed Sacrament.
For many years she told people about this. Eventually the bishop of Liège in 1246 established the feast in his diocese. In 1263, a priest in Bolsena, Italy, who found it hard to believe in the Real Presence, was said to have seen blood dripping from the Host during Mass. The next year Pope Urban IV declared the feast of Corpus Christi for the whole Church. He asked St. Thomas Aquinas to write the prayers and hymns for it.
Juliana died in 1258, before the feast became universal. She helped the Church celebrate the Real Presence.

lessons.title: Receiving Communion
lessons.idea: To receive Communion worthily we believe the Church’s faith, are in the state of grace (free of mortal sin), fast for one hour, and come with reverence. Afterward we give thanks.
lessons.question: How do we prepare?
lessons.activity: “Before and after” prayer cards (25 min). Students write a preparation prayer and a thanksgiving prayer. Practice reverent reception: stepping up, bowing, “Amen,” hands (on tongue or in hands), and moving away. Look at the Anima Christi.
teach: To receive, one must be in the state of grace (CCC 1385). Anyone aware of mortal sin should go to Confession first (CCC 1415; 1 Corinthians 11:27–29).
One hour fast from food and drink (water and medicine excepted) shows respect (Canon 919; CCC 1387). Reverent gestures express faith.
Fruits of Communion: union with Christ, forgiveness of venial sin, preservation from mortal sin, unity of the Church, commitment to the poor (CCC 1391–1397).
Non-Catholics are warmly invited to a blessing or to pray, since reception expresses full communion (CCC 1398–1401).
quiz: The Eucharistic fast is…|Ten minutes|One week|One hour|One day|2|Canon 919.
To receive, one must be…|In a state of grace|A priest|Famous|An adult|0|CCC 1385.
When receiving, we say…|Please|Thanks|Amen|Hello|2|CCC 1389.
lessons.life: Write a prayer to say after Communion.
lessons.saint: Dominic Savio: a boy who prepared for his First Communion with promises he kept.
misc: “If I make a mistake, God will reject me.”
lessons.mem: Soul of Christ, sanctify me; Body of Christ, save me; Blood of Christ, inebriate me. (Anima Christi)
lessons.hook: Ask, “How would you prepare to meet a king?” Then, “Whom do we meet in Communion?” Read 1 Corinthians 11:27–29.
lessons.assess: Ask students to list the four ways to prepare and explain why we say “Amen.”

script.open: Say, “If the President of the country was coming to your house for dinner, what would you do to get ready? Clean, put on nice clothes, think about what to say. Now we are going to receive someone even greater. How should we prepare?”
teach: Read 1 Corinthians 11:27-29. Say: “Paul warns the Christians in Corinth: ‘Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of profaning the body and blood of the Lord. Let a man examine himself, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.’ This is serious: we are receiving Jesus himself.”

Say: “The Church asks us to prepare in four ways. One: believe what the Church teaches about the Eucharist. Two: be in the state of grace. This means we must not have unconfessed mortal sin on our soul. If we are aware of one, we must go to Confession first. Three: fast for at least one hour before Communion from food and drink (water and medicine are allowed). Four: come with reverence, dressed and acting respectfully, with a quiet heart. Genuflect, fold hands, receive with devotion, and say ‘Amen’ with faith.”

Say: “After Communion we give thanks. Jesus is really within us. This is a precious time for silent prayer. We can say, ‘Thank you, Jesus, I love you, help me.’ The Church encourages us to receive Communion often, and at least once a year during the Easter season. We also make a spiritual communion when we cannot receive, asking Jesus to come into our hearts. The fruits of Communion: closer union with Christ, forgiveness of venial sins, protection from mortal sin, unity with the Church, and love for the poor.”
ask: What does ‘state of grace’ mean? (Free from mortal sin, in God’s friendship.)
How long should we fast before Communion? (One hour.)
What do we do after Communion? (Give thanks, pray quietly.)
practice: Fold a card in two. On the left side, write a prayer to say before Communion in your own words (for example, “Jesus, I believe you are here. Make my heart clean.”).
On the right side, write a prayer for after Communion (“Thank you, Jesus, for coming to me. Help me love others.”).
Decorate with a chalice and host.
Read your prayers quietly to yourself.
script.close: Pray together the Act of Spiritual Communion: “My Jesus, I believe that you are present in the Blessed Sacrament.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Use your prayer cards at Mass.”

tryit: Say what you need to be ready.
lessons.saintStory:
Dominic Savio received his First Communion at the age of seven, in 1849, in a village near Turin, Italy. In those days, children usually had to wait until they were older, but Dominic’s priest saw how much he loved Jesus. Dominic prepared with great care. He wrote four promises for the day: “One: I will go to Confession and Communion as often as my confessor permits. Two: I want to sanctify Sundays and feast days. Three: My friends will be Jesus and Mary. Four: Death rather than sin.”
He kept these promises throughout his short life. Dominic also went to Confession regularly, and he made time each day to thank Jesus after Communion. At twelve he met Don Bosco, and joined his school in Turin, and showed his friends how to be good. He died at fourteen.
Dominic shows how to prepare for Communion, and how to give thanks.

lessons.title: The Introductory Rites and Liturgy of the Word
lessons.idea: The Mass begins with the Introductory Rites, where we gather and repent, and the Liturgy of the Word, where God speaks. We hear the first reading, the psalm, the second reading, the Gospel, the homily, then pray the Creed and the Prayer of the Faithful.
lessons.question: What are the readings?
lessons.activity: “Follow the readings” (30 min). Distribute a Sunday missal or a printout of the readings. Students mark first reading, psalm, second reading, Alleluia, Gospel. Practice a response aloud. Then write a one-sentence summary of the Gospel and what it asks.
teach: Gather: entrance song, greeting, Penitential Act, Gloria, Collect (CCC 1348). We stand, sing and prepare our hearts.

Liturgy of the Word: first reading (usually the Old Testament), responsorial psalm, second reading (the letters), Alleluia and Gospel, homily, Creed, Prayer of the Faithful (CCC 1349). At the Gospel we stand because Christ himself speaks.
On Sundays the readings follow a three-year cycle (A, B, C) so that much of the Bible is read over time (CCC 1154).
God’s Word is truly proclaimed, not just read. Encourage students to listen for one line.
quiz: The first reading is usually from…|The Gospels|A letter|A book|The Old Testament|3|CCC 1349.
The homily explains…|The weather|The news|Sports|The readings|3|CCC 1349.
The Gospel is proclaimed by…|A priest or deacon|A child only|Anyone|A choir|0|CCC 1349.
lessons.life: Read next Sunday’s readings beforehand.
lessons.saint: Ezra the scribe: the priest who read God’s word to the people, and who wept for joy.
misc: “The Prayer of the Faithful is just announcements.”
lessons.mem: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.” (Psalm 119:105)
lessons.hook: Ask, “What did you hear at Mass last Sunday?” Read Nehemiah 8:1–12, where the people stood, listened and wept for joy at the reading of the Law.
lessons.assess: Ask students to put the parts of the first half of Mass in order.

script.open: Read a short passage aloud in a very dull, quick voice. Then read the same passage with feeling. Ask, “What is the difference? When God’s word is read well, it can change us.”
teach: Read Nehemiah 8:1-12 in summary. Say: “Ezra read from the book of the Law, all morning. The people listened. The priests explained it. The people wept, and then they rejoiced. This is a picture of the first main part of Mass, the Liturgy of the Word. Jesus says, ‘He who hears you hears me.’ In the readings God speaks to his people.”

Say: “The Mass begins with the Introductory Rites. We gather, sing the entrance song, and the priest greets us. We make the Sign of the Cross. We ask forgiveness in the Penitential Act. We sing ‘Lord, have mercy’ and, on most Sundays, the ‘Glory to God’. And the priest says the Collect, or opening prayer. These rites help us to become a community ready to listen.”

Say: “Then comes the Liturgy of the Word. The first reading is usually from the Old Testament. The responsorial psalm is sung. The second reading is from the New Testament letters. We stand and sing the Gospel Acclamation (the Alleluia). The Gospel is read by the priest or deacon. The homily explains the readings. On Sundays we say the Creed, and we pray the Prayer of the Faithful for the needs of the Church and the world. Over three years, the Sunday readings cover most of the Bible.”
ask: What are the parts of the Introductory Rites? (Entrance, greeting, Penitential Act, Gloria, Collect.)
What are the readings on Sunday? (First reading, psalm, second reading, Gospel.)
Why do we stand for the Gospel? (It is Christ’s own words.)
practice: Give each student a copy of the Sunday readings (or a missal).
Read the Gospel aloud together, and then the first reading.
Each student writes: one word or phrase that stood out, one question, and one thing God might be saying to me today.
Share in pairs.
script.close: Pray: “Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read the Sunday Gospel before Mass.”

tryit: Follow the readings with a missal.
Mark the parts of the Introductory Rites.
Write one thing God says to you.
lessons.saintStory:
After the people of Israel returned from exile in Babylon, they rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. Then, in a great public gathering, Ezra the priest and scribe stood on a wooden platform and read the book of the Law of Moses to them, from early morning until midday.
The Levites helped, explaining the meaning so that all could understand. As people listened, they began to weep, because they realized how much they had neglected God’s word. But Nehemiah and Ezra said to them, “This day is holy to the Lord your God. Do not mourn or weep… Do not be grieved, for the joy of the Lord is your strength.” So they went off to eat and drink and celebrate, because they had understood the words.
This scene is a picture of the Liturgy of the Word at Mass: the word is read, explained, and received with joy.

lessons.title: The Liturgy of the Eucharist
lessons.idea: In the Liturgy of the Eucharist the gifts of bread and wine are prepared, the Eucharistic Prayer is offered, and we receive Holy Communion. The central moment is the consecration.
lessons.question: What happens at the Consecration?
lessons.activity: “Order the steps” relay (25 min). Cards with: Preparation of the gifts, Preface, Sanctus, Epiclesis, Institution narrative, Memorial acclamation, Great Amen, Our Father, Sign of peace, Lamb of God, Communion, Prayer after Communion. Teams put them in order, then explain each one.
teach: Preparation of the gifts: bread and wine are brought forward and offered (CCC 1350). The priest prays that the sacrifice “may be acceptable to God the almighty Father.”

The Eucharistic Prayer is the heart: thanksgiving (Preface), Sanctus, epiclesis (asking the Spirit), institution narrative (the words of Christ), anamnesis (remembering), offering and intercessions (CCC 1352–1354).
Communion Rite: Our Father, sign of peace, breaking of bread (Lamb of God), Communion (CCC 1355). The priest acts “in persona Christi” (CCC 1548).
The Mass makes present the one sacrifice of Calvary in an unbloody manner (CCC 1366–1367).
quiz: The Sanctus is…|Holy, Holy, Holy|Lamb of God|Creed|Our Father|0|CCC 1352.
The institution narrative recounts…|The Last Supper|Pentecost|Creation|Baptism|0|CCC 1353.
The Great Amen follows…|The Gospel|The creed|The homily|The doxology|3|CCC 1353.
lessons.life: Sing the Sanctus with attention.
lessons.saint: Isaiah: the prophet who saw heaven and heard, “Holy, holy, holy.”
misc: “The Mass is a new sacrifice each time.”
lessons.mem: “Do this in remembrance of me.” (Luke 22:19)
lessons.hook: Set a table and bring bread and wine. “What happens at Mass at this table?” Show Luke 22:19.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain epiclesis, institution narrative and communion in their own words.

script.open: Read Isaiah 6:1-3 dramatically. Say, “Imagine being there. This is what we join every time we say ‘Holy, holy, holy’ at Mass.”
teach: Say: “The second main part of the Mass is the Liturgy of the Eucharist. It has three parts. First, the Preparation of the Gifts: bread and wine are brought to the altar, with the collection for the poor. The priest offers them to God. Second, the Eucharistic Prayer, the heart of the Mass. It begins with the Preface, a prayer of thanks. We sing the Holy, Holy, Holy (the Sanctus). The priest asks the Holy Spirit to come upon the gifts (the epiclesis). Then comes the consecration.”

Read Luke 22:19. Say: “At the consecration, the priest says the words of Jesus: ‘Take this, all of you, and eat of it, for this is my Body, which will be given up for you.’ And over the chalice: ‘Take this, all of you, and drink from it, for this is the chalice of my Blood…’ At that moment the bread and wine become Jesus’ Body and Blood. The priest lifts the Host and the chalice, and we adore. The Eucharistic Prayer continues with remembering Christ’s death and Resurrection, praying for the Church, the living and the dead.”

Say: “Third, the Communion Rite. We pray the Our Father together. We offer each other the Sign of Peace. The priest breaks the Host while we sing the Lamb of God. We say, ‘Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed.’ Then we receive Holy Communion. We then pray quietly and the priest says the Prayer after Communion.”
ask: What happens at the consecration? (Bread and wine become Christ’s Body and Blood.)
What do we sing in the Eucharistic Prayer? (Holy, Holy, Holy.)
What do we say before Communion? (Lord, I am not worthy…)
practice: Prepare cards: Preparation of the gifts, Preface, Sanctus, Epiclesis, Consecration, Memorial acclamation, Great Amen, Our Father, Sign of Peace, Lamb of God, Communion, Prayer after Communion.
Teams race to put the cards in order.
Check the order with a missal.
Choose three cards and explain what they mean.
script.close: Pray the Holy, Holy, Holy together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “At Mass, notice when Isaiah’s words are sung.”

tryit: Put the steps of the Liturgy of the Eucharist in order.
lessons.saintStory:
Isaiah was a prophet in Jerusalem about 700 years before Christ. In the year that King Uzziah died, he was in the Temple and had a vision. He saw the Lord sitting on a high throne, and the hem of his robe filled the Temple. Angels called seraphim hovered above, each with six wings, crying to each other, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!”
The doorposts shook, and the house filled with smoke. Isaiah cried, “Woe is me! I am a man of unclean lips.” One of the seraphim flew to him with a burning coal from the altar and touched his mouth, saying, “Your guilt is taken away, and your sin forgiven.” Then he heard the voice of the Lord: “Whom shall I send?” and Isaiah said, “Here I am! Send me.”
At every Mass, in the Eucharistic Prayer, we sing Isaiah’s words: “Holy, holy, holy.” We join the angels as Jesus comes to the altar.

lessons.title: Concluding Rites and mission
lessons.idea: The Concluding Rites bless us and send us out. “Ite, missa est” (“Go, you are sent”) gives the Mass its name. What we receive at Mass we are meant to give away.
lessons.question: What does “Ite, missa est” mean?
lessons.activity: “Sent!” service project (30 min). The class chooses a service project (card writing for the homebound, collecting food, cleaning up the church). Plan jobs, roles and a prayer. Close the planning with the dismissal and blessing.
teach: After Communion come the prayer, announcements, blessing and dismissal (CCC 1332, 1351). The words “Go in peace” or “Go and announce the Gospel of the Lord” send us out.
The Eucharist commits us to the poor (CCC 1397). We cannot receive Christ and ignore him in others (Matthew 25:40).
The Church’s precepts include attending Mass on Sundays and holy days and supporting the Church’s needs (CCC 2041–2043).
Encourage students to think of leaving Mass as the start of an assignment.
quiz: “Mass” comes from…|Message|Mass media|Messiah|Ite, missa est|3|CCC 1332.
The Mass ends with…|A sermon|The Gloria|A blessing and dismissal|Communion|2|CCC 1332.
We are sent to…|Hide|Rest|Wait|Love and serve|3|John 20:21.
lessons.life: After Mass, do one kind thing.
lessons.saint: Teresa of Calcutta: Eucharist leads to service.
lessons.mem: “Go into all the world and proclaim the Gospel to the whole creation.” (Mark 16:15)
lessons.hook: Ask, “What’s the difference between a meeting that ends and a mission that starts?” Read Mark 16:15 and ask who is being sent.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain “Ite, missa est” and name one way they will live out Mass this week.

script.open: Ask the children, “Have you ever got a really good gift and wanted to tell everybody about it?” Take a few answers. “At Mass, we receive the best gift in the world. At the end, the priest tells us what to do with it.”
teach: Say: “The Mass ends with the Concluding Rites. The priest greets us again, and gives a blessing, usually in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Then the deacon or priest sends us out with one of these: ‘Go forth, the Mass is ended,’ or ‘Go in peace, glorifying the Lord by your life,’ or ‘Go in peace.’ We answer, ‘Thanks be to God.’”

Say: “The Latin words are ‘Ite, missa est,’ which literally mean ‘Go, it is the sending.’ The word ‘Mass’ comes from missa, ‘sent.’ So the very name Mass tells us that we are being sent. In Mark 16:15, Jesus told the apostles, ‘Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to the whole creation.’ We too are sent to bring Christ to the world.”

Say: “What we receive at Mass is meant to be given away. We were fed so that we can feed. We were forgiven so that we can forgive. We heard the Word so that we can share it. Jesus said, ‘Whatever you did for one of the least of these my brothers, you did for me.’ The Eucharist and love for the poor go together. The Mass doesn’t end when we leave the church. It continues in how we live the rest of the week.”
ask: What does ‘Ite, missa est’ mean? (Go, you are sent.)
Where does the word ‘Mass’ come from? (From missa, ‘sent.’)
How can we carry the Eucharist into our week? (Serve others, share, forgive.)
practice: As a class, brainstorm service projects: writing cards for people in a nursing home, collecting food, cleaning a parish area, praying for the sick.
Choose one and plan it: who, what, when, and how.
Make or gather what you need.
Carry it out, and reflect on how it connects to the Mass.
script.close: Say together the dismissal: “Go in peace, glorifying the Lord by your life.” Answer: “Thanks be to God.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Do one act of service this week as your ‘mission.’”

tryit: Choose a service project as a class.
lessons.saintStory:
Agnes Gonxha Bojaxhiu was born in 1910, in what is now North Macedonia. She became a Sister of Loreto and taught in Calcutta, India, for nearly twenty years. In 1946, on a train, she felt Jesus call her to serve the poorest of the poor. She left the convent, put on a plain white sari with blue stripes, and went out into the streets of Calcutta.
She started the Missionaries of Charity in 1950. Every day began with Mass and prayer. The sisters spent an hour in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament, and then went out to care for the sick, the dying, the unwanted and the abandoned. Mother Teresa said, “In the Eucharist I see Jesus under the appearance of bread. In the slums I see him in the distressing disguise of the poor.”
She died in 1997 and was named a saint in 2016. Mother Teresa shows that the Eucharist sends us out to serve.

lessons.title: Sin and conversion
lessons.idea: Sin is an offense against God, reason and truth, and it wounds us and others. God calls everyone to conversion, a turning of the heart. Zacchaeus shows what real change looks like.
lessons.question: What is conversion?
lessons.activity: “Zacchaeus in action” (25 min). Act the scene in four frames: the tree, the call, the dinner, the promise. Then write a “return and repair” plan for a modern situation: if I took, I give back; if I hurt, I apologize. Pray the Act of Contrition.
teach: Conversion (metanoia) is a turning to God and away from sin (CCC 1427–1433). It is a gift of grace and demands our response.
Sin is “an offense against reason, truth and right conscience” (CCC 1849). It wounds our nature and harms solidarity (CCC 1849–1853).
Zacchaeus gives half to the poor and repays four times what he stole (Luke 19:8). Real contrition includes making amends.
Stress God’s initiative: Jesus says, “I must stay at your house today.” The Father runs to the prodigal (Luke 15).
quiz: Conversion is…|Changing clothes|Moving house|Winning|Turning toward God|3|CCC 1428.
Zacchaeus promised to…|Complain|Run|Repay and give to the poor|Hide|2|Luke 19:8.
Jesus said, “Today…”|You are late|Salvation has come|Go away|Sit|1|Luke 19:9.
lessons.life: Make a restitution this week if you owe someone.
lessons.saint: Zacchaeus: the tax collector who climbed a tree to see Jesus and gave back what he had taken.
lessons.mem: “Today salvation has come to this house.” (Luke 19:9)
lessons.hook: Ask, “What do you do when you take the wrong turn?” (Turn around.) Read Luke 19:1–10 and ask how Zacchaeus turned around.
lessons.assess: Ask students to retell the Zacchaeus story and name what conversion required.

script.open: Ask a child to quickly stand on a chair. “What can you see from here that you could not see before? Zacchaeus climbed a tree for a good view. Let’s see what he saw.”
teach: Read Luke 19:1-10 aloud. Say: “Zacchaeus was curious. He wanted to see Jesus. But Jesus saw him first, and called him by name. That is how it works with God: he looks for us first.”

Say: “What is sin? Sin is an offense against God, against reason, and against truth. It is a failure in genuine love for God and neighbor. It wounds our nature and harms human solidarity. Every sin damages our relationship with God, with others and with ourselves. Some sins are done, some left undone. They can be in thought, word, deed and omission. We cannot just ignore it.”

Say: “But God calls us to conversion, which means turning around. Conversion starts with God’s grace, as we see with Zacchaeus. Jesus does not wait until he has changed to love him. Jesus’ love changes him. And real conversion shows itself in action: Zacchaeus gave to the poor and paid back what he took. Penance is not just a feeling of sadness. It is a change of life.”
ask: What is sin? (An offense against God, reason and truth; a failure in love.)
What is conversion? (Turning the heart back to God.)
What did Zacchaeus do to show he had changed? (Gave to the poor, paid back four times.)
practice: Choose students to play Zacchaeus, Jesus, the crowd and the poor.
Act out the story in four frames: the tree, the call, the dinner, the change.
In each frame, freeze, and ask the actors what they’re thinking.
Write one sentence about what real change looks like, and share.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, help me to turn to you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Is there something you need to make right? Do it this week.”

tryit: Act out Zacchaeus in four frames.
Say what real change looks like.
lessons.saintStory:
Zacchaeus was the chief tax collector in Jericho, and he was rich. Tax collectors worked for the Romans, and they usually took extra for themselves, so people did not like them. Zacchaeus was also short.
When Jesus came to Jericho, a big crowd lined the streets, and Zacchaeus could not see. So he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree. When Jesus came to the tree, he looked up and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.” Zacchaeus came down at once and welcomed him joyfully. The crowd muttered that Jesus was staying with a sinner.
Zacchaeus said, “Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” Jesus said, “Today salvation has come to this house.” An old tradition says that Zacchaeus later became a bishop. He shows what true conversion is: a change of heart that shows in what we do.

lessons.title: The sacrament of Penance
lessons.idea: The Sacrament of Penance (Reconciliation) has four parts: contrition, confession, satisfaction (penance) and absolution. The priest acts in the person of Christ and is bound to total secrecy.
lessons.question: What are the four parts?
lessons.activity: “Confession walkthrough” (30 min). Mark out a room with stations: examination, contrition (Act of Contrition), confession, penance, absolution, thanksgiving. A volunteer adult plays priest and a student plays penitent with a fictional sin. Debrief on how it felt.
teach: Acts of the penitent: contrition, confession, satisfaction (CCC 1450–1460). Perfect contrition comes from love of God; imperfect from fear or shame (CCC 1451–1453).
Absolution: “I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father…” (CCC 1449). The priest is bound by the sacramental seal, absolutely (CCC 1467).
We must confess all mortal sins, in kind and number; confessing venial sins is recommended (CCC 1456–1458). Receive the sacrament at least once a year (CCC 2042).
Prepare a simple examination for children. Normalize fear and show the joy of forgiveness.
quiz: The four parts: contrition, confession, penance and…|Absolution|Commandment|Conversation|Communion|0|CCC 1450-1460.
The words of absolution include…|I forget you|I absolve you|I judge you|I teach you|1|CCC 1449.
The seal of confession is…|Optional|Absolute|Broken|Shared|1|CCC 1467.
lessons.life: Plan to go to Confession during Advent or Lent.
lessons.saint: Padre Pio: a friar who heard confessions for many hours every day.
misc: “The priest can tell others what I said.”
“If I forget a sin, the confession is invalid.”
lessons.mem: “I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” (Rite of Penance)
lessons.hook: Ask, “Who do you tell when you’ve done something wrong?” Recall John 20:21–23: Jesus gives apostles the power to forgive.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the four parts and the seal of confession.

script.open: Have two cups: one clean, one muddy. Say, “Imagine drinking out of these. Which would you choose? Sin makes our soul like the muddy cup. The sacrament of Penance cleans it.”
teach: Read John 20:23. Say: “On Easter evening, Jesus breathed on the apostles and said, ‘If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.’ The Church has always understood that this power continued with bishops and priests. In Penance, a priest acts in the person of Christ, the Head. That is why we confess our sins to a priest, and not only to God.”

Say: “The sacrament has four parts. One: contrition: sorrow for our sins and a firm purpose not to sin again. Perfect contrition comes from love of God. Imperfect contrition comes from fear of punishment or the ugliness of sin, and it is enough for the sacrament. Two: confession: telling our sins to the priest. We must confess all mortal sins we remember, in kind and number. It’s also good to confess venial sins. Three: satisfaction, or penance: the priest gives us a prayer or act to repair the harm and to heal. Four: absolution: the priest says, ‘I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’”

Say: “The priest is bound by the seal of confession. He can never reveal what he has heard. Nothing, not the law, not any person, can make him. Priests have died rather than break it. Why Confession? Because it gives us certainty that we are forgiven, helps us to name our sins honestly, and restores us to the Church. It also brings peace. Pope Francis called it ‘a hug from God.’ We should go regularly, and especially before we receive Communion with a mortal sin.”
ask: What are the four parts of Penance? (Contrition, confession, satisfaction, absolution.)
Why do we go to a priest? (He acts in the person of Christ, as Jesus gave the apostles the power.)
What is the seal of confession? (The priest may never reveal what he hears.)
practice: Set up stations around the room: Examine your conscience (a list of questions), Be sorry (the Act of Contrition), Confess (a mock confessional with two chairs), Receive penance (a card), Absolution (the words of absolution).
Walk through each station, one at a time.
At the “confessional,” practice the opening words: “Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It has been ___ since my last confession.”
Say the Act of Contrition aloud together.
script.close: Pray the Act of Contrition. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Plan to go to Confession as a family.”

tryit: Walk through the stations of Confession.
Say what you do at each.
lessons.saintStory:
Francesco Forgione was born in Italy in 1887. He became a Capuchin friar and took the name Pio. In 1916 he went to live at a friary in San Giovanni Rotondo, a small town in the mountains, and stayed there for over fifty years.
In 1918 people began to say that he had the wounds of Christ, the stigmata, on his hands, feet and side. This brought huge crowds to see him. But Padre Pio gave most of his time to something else: hearing confessions. He sat in the confessional for ten, twelve, even fourteen hours a day. People waited days to see him. Many said that he seemed to know their sins before they told him, and that they came out feeling a great peace.
He also said Mass with great reverence and started a hospital, the House for the Relief of Suffering. He died in 1968. Padre Pio shows what the sacrament of Penance is: mercy given through a priest.

lessons.title: Anointing of the Sick
lessons.idea: In the Anointing of the Sick, a priest anoints the forehead and hands with oil of the sick and prays, giving strength, peace and courage in serious illness or old age. It may also give physical healing if God wills.
lessons.question: When is it celebrated?
lessons.activity: “Visit and pray” (25 min). Students write cards for the sick and practice words of comfort. Role-play a priest’s visit with oil of the sick. Learn the prayers: “Through this holy anointing may the Lord in his love and mercy help you with the grace of the Holy Spirit.”
teach: James 5:14–15 describes the practice: elders anoint with oil and pray, and the Lord raises up and forgives (CCC 1499–1513).
The sacrament is for those who are seriously ill or weakened by age, and it can be repeated if the illness worsens (CCC 1514–1515). It is not only for the dying.
Its effects: strength, peace, forgiveness of sins, union with Christ’s Passion, sometimes bodily healing (CCC 1520–1523). The Viaticum (Communion for the dying) completes it (CCC 1524–1525).
Speak sensitively. Some students have ill relatives. Offer hope.
talk: How can you comfort the sick?
quiz: Anointing uses…|Water|Salt|Bread|Oil of the sick|3|CCC 1513.
It may be received…|More than once|By priests only|Never|Once only|0|CCC 1515.
It is celebrated for…|Serious illness or old age|Games|Colds|Exams|0|CCC 1514.
lessons.life: Visit or write to someone who is sick.
lessons.saint: Marianne Cope: a sister who cared for people with leprosy on Molokai.
misc: “Last rites mean you’re about to die.”
“If the person isn’t healed, the sacrament failed.”
lessons.mem: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church.” (James 5:14)
lessons.hook: Ask who has been in the hospital or visited someone. “How do you show care?” Read James 5:14–15.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain who may receive the sacrament and its effects.

script.open: Ask, “Have you ever been sick for a long time, or visited someone who was? What helped? Did you wish for something to make you feel better?” Take answers. “God has a sacrament for exactly this.”
teach: Read James 5:14-15. Say: “‘Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick man, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.’ From the first days of the Church, Christians have prayed for their sick and anointed them with oil.”

Say: “The Anointing of the Sick is given to someone who is seriously ill, or facing surgery, or growing weak from old age. It can be received more than once, if the illness gets worse or returns. The priest lays hands on the person, anoints the forehead and hands with the oil of the sick, and prays: ‘Through this holy anointing may the Lord in his love and mercy help you with the grace of the Holy Spirit. May the Lord who frees you from sin save you and raise you up.’”

Say: “What does it do? It gives strength, peace and courage to face illness or old age. It unites the person to Christ’s suffering. It forgives sins if the person could not go to Confession. It sometimes brings healing of the body, if it is God’s will, but the main healing is of the soul. It also prepares a person for the final journey. When someone is dying, the Church also gives Viaticum, which means ‘food for the journey,’ the Eucharist received for the last time. The sacrament is not only for the dying. It is for anyone who needs strength.”
ask: Who can receive the Anointing of the Sick? (Anyone seriously ill, or weak from old age.)
What does the priest anoint? (Forehead and hands.)
What is Viaticum? (The Eucharist received at the end of life: food for the journey.)
practice: Give each student a card and markers.
Write a message to someone who is ill or lonely (a grandparent, a neighbor, someone in a hospital or nursing home).
Practice kind, simple words of comfort: “I am thinking of you. I am praying for you.”
Pray a decade of the Rosary or an Our Father for the sick as a group, then deliver the cards.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, bless and heal the sick.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Visit or call someone who is sick.”

lessons.saintStory:
Barbara Cope was born in Germany in 1838 and moved with her family to Utica, New York, when she was a baby. She worked in a factory to help her family until she was old enough to join the Sisters of St. Francis in Syracuse, where she took the name Marianne. She became a teacher, a nurse, and then the head of her community. She helped start two of the first hospitals in central New York.
In 1883, she received a letter from the king of Hawaii, asking for sisters to care for people with leprosy, a disease from which many people shrank in fear. Many other communities had refused. Mother Marianne wrote back, “I am hungry for the work… I will cheerfully accept the work.” She went with six other sisters to Hawaii, where she lived for thirty-five years, caring for patients on the island of Molokai. She cared for Father Damien when he was dying.
Marianne died in 1918, and was named a saint in 2012. She shows how love can reach the sick, and why the Church anoints them.

units.title: Holy Orders and Matrimony
units.eq: How do the sacraments serve others?

lessons.title: Holy Orders
lessons.idea: In Holy Orders Christ continues his priesthood through bishops, priests and deacons. Ordination marks the soul and configures the man to Christ the head and shepherd.
lessons.question: Who can be ordained?
lessons.activity: “Ministry interview” (30 min). Invite a priest or deacon (or watch a short interview) and let students ask prepared questions about his call and daily life. Draw the three degrees of Orders with their roles.
teach: Holy Orders has three degrees: bishop, priest, deacon (CCC 1554, 1536). Bishops are successors of the apostles. Priests are co-workers of bishops. Deacons serve in word, liturgy and charity (CCC 1555–1571).
Ordination imprints an indelible character and makes the priest act in persona Christi capitis (CCC 1548, 1581–1584). Jesus chose the Twelve (Luke 6:12–16) and the Church ordains only men (CCC 1577).
The minister of ordination is a bishop through the laying on of hands and the prayer of consecration (CCC 1572–1574).
Celibacy in the Latin Church is a discipline, not a doctrine; Eastern Churches ordain married men (CCC 1579–1580).
quiz: Holy Orders has…|One degree|Two degrees|Three degrees|Five degrees|2|CCC 1554.
The ordinary minister of ordination is…|A priest|A bishop|A layperson|A deacon|1|CCC 1576.
Priests act…|As kings|In the person of Christ|As teachers only|On their own|1|CCC 1548.
lessons.life: Pray for priests every day.
lessons.saint: Michael McGivney: a parish priest who started the Knights of Columbus to help families.
lessons.mem: “Do this in remembrance of me.” (Luke 22:19)
lessons.hook: Ask, “Who leads a team, serves at a table and shepherds a flock?” Each image fits a role: bishop, deacon, priest.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name the three degrees and one duty of each.

script.open: Ask, “If you could ask a priest or a deacon any question, what would it be?” Write the questions on the board. Say, “We’ll use these in an interview.”
teach: Say: “Holy Orders is the sacrament in which Christ continues his own priesthood through his chosen ministers. It has three degrees. Bishops are the successors of the apostles. They lead a diocese, ordain priests and deacons, and confirm. Priests are the bishop’s co-workers. They preach, celebrate Mass, hear confessions and anoint the sick. Deacons assist at Mass, proclaim the Gospel, preach, baptize, witness marriages and serve the poor.”

Read Luke 22:19: “Do this in memory of me.” Say: “At the Last Supper, Jesus gave the apostles the command to do what he had done. The apostles passed on their ministry by the laying on of hands to others. This unbroken chain is called apostolic succession.
