In the sacrament of Holy Orders, the bishop lays hands on the man and prays for the Holy Spirit. The man is changed: he is marked forever. A priest acts ‘in persona Christi capitis’, in the person of Christ the Head.”

Say: “Only baptized men are ordained, following Jesus’ choice of the Twelve and the Church’s constant tradition. Most priests in the Latin Church promise celibacy, which means not marrying, to give themselves entirely to Christ and the Church. Eastern Catholic churches can ordain married men to the priesthood. Every priest was first a boy in a parish like ours. We pray for vocations. And we respect and thank our priests and deacons.”
ask: What are the three degrees of Holy Orders? (Bishop, priest, deacon.)
What does a priest do? (Celebrates Mass, hears confessions, anoints the sick, preaches.)
What does ‘in the person of Christ’ mean? (The priest acts as Christ acts through him.)
practice: Invite a priest or a deacon to answer student questions, or watch a short interview video.
Beforehand, work together to choose the five best questions: How did you know you were called? What is your favorite part of the day?
Take notes during the interview.
Afterward, each student writes one thing that surprised them and one thing they’ll pray for the priest.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, bless our priests, deacons and bishops.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Thank a priest or deacon this week.”

tryit: Prepare questions for a priest or deacon.
lessons.saintStory:
Michael McGivney was born in 1852 in Waterbury, Connecticut, the oldest of thirteen children, to Irish immigrants. He left school at thirteen to work in a factory to help his family, but later went to seminary, and was ordained in 1877. He served at St. Mary’s Church in New Haven.
He saw that when a father in a parish died, the family often fell into poverty. Many Catholic men also joined secret societies that were against the Church for the insurance benefits. In 1882 he gathered a group of men in the church basement and started the Knights of Columbus, a Catholic fraternal organization to help families, strengthen faith and care for widows and orphans.
Father McGivney died of pneumonia in 1890, at thirty-eight. He was beatified in 2020. He shows what a priest does: serve, listen, and build up his people.

lessons.title: Matrimony
lessons.idea: In Matrimony a baptized man and woman make a covenant for life, ordered to their good and to children. It is a sacrament and a sign of Christ’s love for the Church.
lessons.question: What are the goods of marriage?
lessons.activity: “Wedding rite” (25 min). Walk through the rite: the entrance, readings, exchange of consent, rings, nuptial blessing. Students underline the vows. Compare with Jesus’ words in Matthew 19:4–6.
teach: Marriage was created by God and raised by Christ to a sacrament (CCC 1601–1617). The couple are the ministers; the priest or deacon witnesses (CCC 1623).
Four goods: unity, fidelity, indissolubility, openness to children (CCC 1643–1654). “What God has joined together, let no one put asunder” (Mark 10:9).
Marriage is a sign of Christ and the Church (Ephesians 5:25–32; CCC 1616). The family is “the domestic church” (CCC 1655–1658).
Be mindful of students whose families have experienced divorce. Speak with compassion and avoid blame.
talk: What are the goods of marriage?
quiz: The ministers of marriage are…|The parents|The priest|The witnesses|The couple|3|CCC 1623.
Marriage is…|Legal only|Temporary|Optional|Permanent|3|CCC 1640.
The family is…|A team|A club|The domestic church|A business|2|CCC 1655.
lessons.life: Thank a married couple you know.
lessons.saint: Priscilla and Aquila: a married couple who worked with Paul and opened their home to the Church.
misc: “A married couple can cancel a sacramental marriage.”
lessons.mem: “What therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder.” (Mark 10:9)
lessons.hook: Show wedding photos or a ring. Read Genesis 2:18–24 and ask, “What did God see that was not good?” (being alone).
lessons.assess: Ask students to name the four goods and the ministers of the sacrament.

script.open: Ask, “What is a wedding? What happens? Why do people make promises on that day?” Write answers on the board. “Marriage is a sacrament, and a sign of God’s love.”
teach: Read Genesis 2:18-24. Say: “God said, ‘It is not good that the man should be alone.’ He made a woman, and the man said, ‘This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.’ And the text says, ‘Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and cleaves to his wife, and they become one flesh.’ Marriage is God’s idea. It is a covenant, a sacred promise that makes them a family.”

Say: “In the sacrament of Matrimony, a baptized man and woman make a covenant for life. By their free consent, they give themselves to each other. They promise to be faithful, to love each other for life, and to be open to children. Marriage is ordered to the good of the spouses and to the procreation and education of children. It is a sign of Christ’s love for his Church: faithful, free, total and fruitful. Paul wrote about this in Ephesians 5.”

Say: “In the Latin Church, the bride and groom are the ministers of the sacrament. The priest or deacon is the Church’s official witness. The rite includes the entrance, the readings, the questions, the exchange of consent, the blessing and exchange of rings, the nuptial blessing, and often a Mass. The couple promise to take each other ‘for better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health, until death do us part.’ Marriage is a lifelong, faithful and fruitful union. God’s grace helps the couple become holy together.”
ask: What is marriage? (A covenant between a baptized man and woman, for life.)
What do the spouses promise? (Faithfulness, love for life, openness to children.)
What does marriage signify? (Christ’s love for the Church.)
practice: Walk through the wedding rite on cards: entrance, readings, questions, exchange of consent, blessing and exchange of rings, nuptial blessing, Mass.
Students place them in order and say what each means.
In pairs, rewrite the vows in your own words, as a promise to a friend, family member or teammate.
Share one.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, bless every married couple.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask your parents about their wedding.”

tryit: Say the vows in your own words.
lessons.saintStory:
Priscilla and Aquila were a Jewish couple who lived in Rome, and then in Corinth, Ephesus and Rome again. They were tentmakers by trade, as was Paul, so when Paul came to Corinth, he stayed with them and worked alongside them.
They became close friends and co-workers of Paul. They traveled with him to Ephesus, and when a gifted preacher named Apollos came who knew only part of the Gospel, Priscilla and Aquila took him aside and explained the way of God more accurately. Paul wrote in his letter to the Romans, “Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life.” He added, “and the church in their house.”
Their marriage was a partnership in faith, work and ministry. Priscilla and Aquila show how marriage is a vocation to serve God together.

lessons.title: Vocation
lessons.idea: Everyone has a vocation: first the call to holiness and then a particular way to live it, as a married person, a priest or deacon, a consecrated religious, or a dedicated single. We discern through prayer, Scripture, sacraments and wise guidance.
lessons.question: What is your call?
lessons.activity: “Listening for the call” (25 min). Students write a vocation prayer, “Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.” They list gifts they have, needs they see, and someone who could help them discern. Pray it silently for two minutes.
teach: All are called to holiness (CCC 825, 2013). Each person also has a particular vocation: marriage, priesthood, consecrated life, single life lived for God (CCC 914–933, 1877–1879).
God calls through our gifts, circumstances, the Church and conscience. Prayer, the sacraments and spiritual guidance help us hear (CCC 2230–2232).
Parents should foster vocations (CCC 2232). Pray especially for vocations to the priesthood and religious life.
Avoid pressure. Tell students to be open and generous, without anxiety about timing.
quiz: Every Christian is called to…|Fame|Silence|Holiness|Wealth|2|CCC 2013.
Vocation means…|Plan|Call|Job|Hobby|1|Latin vocare.
Discernment involves…|Luck|Coin flips|Prayer and advice|Guessing|2|CCC 2030.
lessons.life: Write a prayer for your vocation.
lessons.saint: Samuel: “Speak, Lord.”
misc: “God has a secret plan I might miss.”
lessons.mem: “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:9)
lessons.hook: Read 1 Samuel 3:1–10. Ask: “Why did Samuel not recognize the voice? Who helped him?” Eli. “We too need help to hear.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name the four vocations and one step toward discerning.

script.open: Ask, “What do you want to be when you grow up? Think of something. Now, what if God has a plan for you? What if he is calling you by name?”
teach: Say: “Vocation comes from the Latin word for ‘call.’ Everyone has a vocation, a call from God. First, God calls us all to holiness, to love him and others and to be with him forever. That’s the call of Baptism. Then he calls each person to a particular way of living it. In 1 Samuel 3:1-10, God called Samuel in the night. Samuel didn’t recognize it at first. We too may not recognize God’s voice at first.”

Say: “There are four main ways to live out our call. Married life: a man and woman who give themselves to each other and their children. Priesthood or diaconate: men who serve the Church through Holy Orders. Consecrated religious life: sisters, brothers and others who vow to live poverty, chastity and obedience for the Kingdom, in community. And dedicated single life: people who serve God and others without marrying, as lay missionaries, teachers, nurses, and so on. All are good, and all are ways to love.”

Say: “How do we discern, or find out, our calling? We pray and listen. We study Scripture. We receive the sacraments, especially Reconciliation and the Eucharist. We ask advice from parents, priests and mentors. We look at our gifts and desires. We serve others. And we trust that God will give us what we need. We don’t have to know everything now. God’s call often comes step by step. You can say what Samuel said: ‘Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.’”
ask: What does ‘vocation’ mean? (A call.)
What is the first call that everyone has? (To holiness.)
How do we discern our vocation? (Prayer, Scripture, sacraments, advice, serving.)
practice: Light a candle and sit in a quiet circle.
Read 1 Samuel 3:1-10 slowly.
Each student writes a short prayer: “Speak, Lord, your servant is listening. Help me to hear you, and to follow where you lead me.”
After three minutes of silence, share one phrase from a prayer.
script.close: Pray the vocation prayer together: “Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray each night: Lord, what do you want me to do?”

lessons.saintStory:
Samuel was a boy dedicated to God. His mother, Hannah, had prayed for a child, and she promised to give him to the Lord. So when he was small, he went to live in the sanctuary at Shiloh with the priest Eli. He wore a little linen ephod and helped in the temple.
One night, as he lay down to sleep, he heard a voice call his name. He ran to Eli, saying, “Here I am, for you called me.” Eli said he had not called. This happened three times. Then Eli realized that the Lord was calling the boy. He told Samuel, “Go and lie down, and if he calls you, you shall say, ‘Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.’” Samuel did, and God gave him a message.
Samuel grew up to be a prophet and a judge, and he anointed the first two kings of Israel, Saul and David. He shows us what a vocation sounds like: God calls by name, and we listen.

lessons.title: The Law of love
lessons.idea: Jesus gives the New Law, the law of love. It fulfills the Old Law, is written on our hearts by the Spirit, and is summarized in the Sermon on the Mount and the Beatitudes.
lessons.question: What is the New Law?
lessons.activity: “Old Law, New Law” (25 min). Two-column chart comparing Old Law (e.g., “Do not kill”) and the New Law (“Do not even be angry; be reconciled”) using Matthew 5:21–48. Discuss: why is the second harder and more freeing? Add Jesus’ new commandment (John 13:34).
teach: The New Law is the grace of the Holy Spirit given in Christ, the perfection of the Old (CCC 1965–1966). It is a law of love, grace and freedom (CCC 1972).
The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) is its charter (CCC 1966). Jesus gives a “new commandment”: “Love one another as I have loved you” (John 13:34; CCC 1970).
The Law is not abolished but fulfilled (Matthew 5:17). The moral life is a response to love, not only obedience to rules (CCC 1972–1974).
Work with children to apply it to ordinary conflicts.
talk: How is it different from the Old?
quiz: The New Law is…|The Law of love|The Law of fear|A tax|A list of fines|0|CCC 1965.
It is written…|On our hearts by the Spirit|In books only|In stone only|In the sand|0|CCC 1966.
The Old Law…|Is evil|Prepares for the Gospel|Is outdated|Has no value|1|CCC 1963.
lessons.life: Practice one Sermon on the Mount teaching.
lessons.saint: Oscar Romero: an archbishop who spoke for the poor and was killed at Mass.
misc: “God of the Old Testament was cruel.”
lessons.mem: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you.” (John 13:34)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What’s the difference between a rule and a relationship?” A rule says what to avoid; love asks what more I can give.
lessons.assess: Ask students to compare an Old Law command and Jesus’ deepening of it.

script.open: Write on the board two lists: “Don’t” and “Do.” Ask students to name some rules at home or school. Say, “Are rules only about what we should not do? Let’s see what Jesus says.”
teach: Read Matthew 22:37-40. Say: “The greatest commandment is, ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart… And you shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ This sums up the whole law. The Old Law is the law God gave Moses: the Ten Commandments and other rules. It is holy and good, but it could not give the grace to keep it.”

Say: “Jesus gives the New Law, the law of love. He didn’t abolish the Old Law. He said, ‘I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it.’ (Matthew 5:17) In the Sermon on the Mount, he deepens it. The Old Law says, ‘You shall not kill.’ Jesus says, ‘Do not even be angry with your brother.’ The Old Law says, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ Jesus says, ‘Do not look at someone with lust.’ The Old Law says, ‘An eye for an eye.’ Jesus says, ‘Love your enemies.’ The New Law goes to the heart.”

Say: “And the New Law is different in another way: it is written on our hearts by the Holy Spirit. We are given the grace to live it. In Jeremiah 31:33, God promised, ‘I will put my law within them, and I will write it upon their hearts.’ The New Law is summed up in the Beatitudes and the Sermon on the Mount. It is also called the law of freedom, because the Spirit moves us to do what is good out of love, not just out of fear.”
ask: What are the two great commandments? (Love God and love your neighbor.)
How is the New Law different from the Old? (It goes to the heart, and the Spirit gives grace to live it.)
Where do we find the heart of the New Law? (The Sermon on the Mount and the Beatitudes.)
practice: Draw a two-column chart: Old Law and New Law.
Fill in rows: “You shall not kill” vs. “Do not be angry; reconcile”; “Do not swear falsely” vs. “Let your yes be yes”; “An eye for an eye” vs. “Love your enemies.”
Choose one row, and write what it looks like in daily life.
Share a challenge.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, write your law on our hearts.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pick one New Law challenge this week.”

tryit: Compare Old Law and New Law.
See how Jesus fulfills each commandment.
Pick a commandment to live more fully.
lessons.saintStory:
Oscar Romero was born in 1917 in El Salvador, and became a priest, then a bishop. In 1977 he was named archbishop of San Salvador, the capital. At the time his country was torn by violence, and many poor people were being killed or taken away. At first Romero seemed quiet and cautious.
Then, in 1977, a priest and friend, Rutilio Grande, was killed because he defended the poor. Romero changed. He started to speak out. Every Sunday he preached in the cathedral and his homilies were broadcast on the radio across the country. He named the victims, and called for an end to violence. He said to the soldiers, “No soldier is obliged to obey an order against the law of God.”
On March 24, 1980, while he was saying Mass in a hospital chapel, he was shot and killed. He was named a saint in 2018. Romero lived the New Law of love, even at the cost of his life.

lessons.title: Mortal and venial sin
lessons.idea: Not all sins are equal. Mortal sin destroys love in the heart by a grave violation of God’s law and requires three things: grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent. Venial sin weakens love but does not break our friendship with God.
lessons.question: What makes a sin mortal?
lessons.activity: “Sort and discuss” (25 min). Under teacher guidance, sort anonymous examples into questions: Is the matter grave? Did the person know? Did they freely choose? Discuss why intention and knowledge matter. Close by praying the Act of Contrition and noting God’s mercy.
teach: Mortal sin requires grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent (CCC 1857). It turns us away from God and needs Confession (CCC 1855–1861).
Venial sin offends but does not kill charity (CCC 1862–1863). Repeated venial sin can lead us toward mortal sin, so we should resist it.
Be careful to address anxiety: those who are worried about their sins are usually not in mortal sin. Encourage trust in God’s mercy (CCC 1864).
Sin has social effects (CCC 1869).
quiz: Mortal sin destroys…|Sleep|Friendship only|Charity in the heart|Nothing|2|CCC 1855.
Which is a condition of mortal sin?|Being tired|Being young|Having money|Full knowledge|3|CCC 1857.
Venial sin…|Is mortal|Is harmless|Wounds but doesn’t destroy charity|Is forgiven automatically|2|CCC 1855.
lessons.life: Learn the Act of Contrition by heart.
lessons.saint: Faustina Kowalska: a sister who spread trust in God’s mercy.
lessons.mem: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, and will forgive our sins.” (1 John 1:9)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Is a scratch the same as a broken leg?” Both hurt, but they need different care. Read 1 John 5:16–17.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the three conditions for mortal sin.

script.open: Ask, “If you broke your friend’s toy by accident, versus on purpose after being told not to touch it, is that the same? Why not?” Take answers. “That helps us understand how sins differ.”
teach: Read 1 John 5:16-17. Say: “John writes, ‘There is sin that is mortal and sin that is not.’ Sin is any thought, word, deed or omission against God’s law. Not all sins have the same weight. Venial sin weakens our love and harms our friendship with God, but doesn’t destroy it. Examples might be a small lie, being lazy, or an unkind word. We need forgiveness for these too, and they are forgiven in the Mass and prayer, and Confession is recommended.”

Say: “Mortal sin is a grave break with God. It destroys love in our hearts and cuts us off from God’s life, which we call sanctifying grace. If we died in mortal sin without repentance, we would be separated from God forever. Three things must all be present for a sin to be mortal. One: grave matter. The act itself is seriously wrong, such as murder, adultery, serious theft or deliberately missing Sunday Mass. Two: full knowledge. We know it is seriously wrong. Three: deliberate consent. We freely choose it. If one is missing, the sin may be less serious.”

Say: “Mortal sin can be forgiven through the sacrament of Reconciliation. If we have committed a mortal sin, we should go to Confession as soon as we can and not receive Communion until we have. But we should never despair. God’s mercy is greater than any sin. As the Lord told Faustina, ‘The greater the sinner, the greater the right he has to my mercy.’ We trust in the mercy of Jesus and do our best to avoid sin.”
ask: What are the three conditions for mortal sin? (Grave matter, full knowledge, deliberate consent.)
What does venial sin do? (Weakens our love but does not destroy it.)
What should we do after a mortal sin? (Go to Confession as soon as possible.)
practice: Prepare anonymous examples written on cards (for instance: “forgetting a prayer,” “cheating on a big test,” “missing Mass on purpose without reason,” “taking a pencil by mistake”).
As a class, discuss them: Is the matter grave? Did the person know? Did they freely choose?
Sort them into a spectrum: no sin, venial, possibly mortal.
End by reading aloud: “Jesus, I trust in you.”
script.close: Pray the Divine Mercy prayer: “Jesus, I trust in you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray ‘Jesus, I trust in you’ every day this week.”

tryit: Sort the examples with your teacher.
lessons.saintStory:
Helena Kowalska was born in Poland in 1905, the third of ten children in a poor farming family. She had only about three years of school and went to work as a housekeeper to help her family. At twenty, she entered a convent and became Sister Faustina.
She worked as a cook, a gardener and a porter. In 1931, she said Jesus appeared to her in a white robe with two rays of light shining from his heart, one red and one pale. He asked her to have an image painted with the words “Jesus, I trust in you.” He asked that the Sunday after Easter be a feast of mercy. Faustina wrote down what Jesus said in a diary. She died of tuberculosis in 1938, at thirty-three.
Pope John Paul II named her a saint in 2000, and established Divine Mercy Sunday. Faustina shows how to trust in God’s mercy, even when we have sinned.

lessons.title: Works of mercy
lessons.idea: Works of mercy are loving actions to help people in body and soul. There are seven corporal and seven spiritual. Jesus says we will be judged on how we treated the least of his brothers and sisters.
lessons.question: Which work will you do this month?
lessons.activity: “Mercy project” (30 min). Make a chart of the 14 works with a local example for each. Choose one for a class project (a food drive, visiting the elderly, a prayer chain). Set dates and assign roles.
teach: The corporal works: feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, shelter the homeless, visit the sick, visit the imprisoned, bury the dead (CCC 2447).
The spiritual works: instruct the ignorant, counsel the doubtful, admonish sinners, comfort the sorrowing, forgive offenses, bear wrongs patiently, pray for the living and the dead (CCC 2447).
“As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40). Our love of the poor is a test of faith (CCC 2443–2446).
Add Catholic social teaching in simple form: dignity, family, solidarity, care for creation.
talk: Which work of mercy can you do?
quiz: A corporal work of mercy is…|Feed the hungry|Pray for the dead|Counsel the doubtful|Forgive offenses|0|CCC 2447.
A spiritual work of mercy is…|Instruct the ignorant|Bury the dead|Visit the sick|Clothe the naked|0|CCC 2447.
Jesus says, “Whatever you did for the least…”|You did for me|Was easy|Was fine|You did for them|0|Matthew 25:40.
lessons.life: Do one work of mercy this week.
lessons.saint: Lawrence of Rome: a deacon who said the poor were the Church’s treasure.
misc: “Someone else will take care of it.”
lessons.mem: “As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” (Matthew 25:40)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 25:31–46 aloud. Ask: “Where was Jesus in the story?” Note the surprise: “I was hungry and you fed me.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name three corporal and three spiritual works and give an example each.

script.open: Show a treasure chest. Ask, “What would you put in a treasure chest? What does the Church treasure most?” Take answers. “A saint answered this question in a very surprising way.”
teach: Read Matthew 25:31-46 in summary. Say: “Jesus describes the Last Judgment. The King says to those on his right, ‘I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me, I was naked and you clothed me, I was sick and you visited me, I was in prison and you came to me.’ They ask, ‘When did we see you?’ He says, ‘As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.’ Then to those on the left he says the opposite. We will be judged on love.”

Say: “The Church has named seven corporal works of mercy, which help the body: feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, shelter the homeless, visit the sick, visit the imprisoned, bury the dead. And seven spiritual works of mercy, which help the soul: instruct the ignorant, counsel the doubtful, admonish sinners, bear wrongs patiently, forgive offenses willingly, comfort the afflicted, pray for the living and the dead.”

Say: “Mercy is love in action, especially for those in need. It means seeing the person in front of us as Jesus. We do not have to do all of them at once. We can start where we are: share lunch with someone who forgot theirs, invite someone who is alone, visit a grandparent, pray for people who are sad, forgive someone who has been unkind. The works of mercy are a way of living out our baptism.”
ask: How many corporal works of mercy are there? (Seven.) Spiritual? (Seven.)
How will Jesus judge us? (On how we treated the least of his brothers and sisters.)
What’s one work of mercy you can do this week? (Take answers.)
practice: Make a chart with the fourteen works of mercy in two columns.
For each, write a local example: for instance, “Feed the hungry: donate to the food pantry.”
As a class, choose one work to do together as a project this week.
Plan: who will do what, and when.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, let me see you in the poor, and serve them.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Do one work of mercy and tell us about it.”

tryit: Add a local example for each.
lessons.saintStory:
Lawrence was one of seven deacons of the Church of Rome in the third century, when Pope Sixtus II led the Church. Deacons helped with the poor and managed the Church’s money and goods, which were used to feed hundreds of poor people in the city.
In the year 258 the emperor ordered that all Christian bishops, priests and deacons be killed. When Pope Sixtus was arrested, Lawrence followed him, weeping and saying he wanted to go with him. The pope told him that he would follow him in three days. In the meantime, the Roman prefect, who thought the Church was rich, ordered Lawrence to bring him the treasures of the Church.
Lawrence gathered the poor, the blind, the lame and the orphans, and presented them, saying, “These are the treasures of the Church.” He was put to death for his faith. Lawrence shows what the works of mercy mean: in the poor, we meet Christ.

lessons.title: The Liturgy of the Hours
lessons.idea: The Liturgy of the Hours is the Church’s daily prayer. Morning Prayer and Evening Prayer are its hinges. It sanctifies the day with psalms, canticles and readings.
lessons.question: What are the hours?
lessons.activity: “Morning Prayer together” (25 min). Pray a short Morning Prayer: opening versicle, hymn, psalm with antiphon, short reading, Benedictus or Magnificat, intercessions, Our Father, blessing. Debrief how the psalms feel.
teach: The Liturgy of the Hours extends the praise of the Eucharist throughout the day (CCC 1174–1178). Priests, religious and many laypeople pray it.
Its core is the Psalms, the prayer of Jesus (CCC 2585–2589). The hours include Office of Readings, Morning, Daytime, Evening and Night Prayer.
Praying the Hours unites us with the whole Church worldwide, who pray in the same rhythm.
Introduce apps or Divine Office books.
quiz: The Liturgy of the Hours is…|A game|A TV show|The Church’s daily prayer|A school subject|2|CCC 1174.
The chief hours are…|None|Noon only|Morning and Evening Prayer|Midnight only|2|CCC 1175.
The main text is…|Letters|The Psalms|Songs|Poems|1|CCC 1177.
lessons.life: Pray a short morning prayer from the Office.
lessons.saint: Columba: an Irish monk who prayed the Psalms and brought the Gospel to Scotland.
misc: “The Liturgy of the Hours is only for priests.”
lessons.mem: “Seven times a day I praise you for your righteous ordinances.” (Psalm 119:164)
lessons.hook: Ask, “How often do you check the time? How often do you think of God?” Read Psalm 119:164: “Seven times a day I praise you.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name two hours of prayer and what they contain.

script.open: Ring a small bell or play a church bell recording. Ask, “What did bells tell people long ago? The hours of the day. Monks stopped what they were doing at certain times to pray. We still do it today.”
teach: Say: “The Church prays not only at Mass, but throughout the day. This prayer is called the Liturgy of the Hours, or the Divine Office. It is the daily prayer of the Church, said by priests, deacons, religious and many lay people. Psalm 119:164 says, ‘Seven times a day I praise you.’ And Paul writes, ‘Pray without ceasing.’”

Say: “The two ‘hinges’ of the Hours are Morning Prayer (Lauds) and Evening Prayer (Vespers). Other hours include the Office of Readings, Daytime Prayer, and Night Prayer (Compline). Each hour is made of psalms, canticles, a short reading, intercessions and a closing prayer. The psalms are the main part. Jesus prayed them. The hours sanctify the day: in the morning we praise God for the new day, in the evening we thank him.”

Say: “It’s a prayer of the whole Church, in union with Christ. Even when you pray it alone, you pray with everyone else who is praying it at that moment. Anyone can pray the Hours, and there are apps and books that make it easy. A simple pattern for Morning Prayer: an opening versicle (‘Lord, open my lips’ / ‘And my mouth will proclaim your praise’), a hymn, a psalm, a short reading, the Canticle of Zechariah (Benedictus), intercessions, the Our Father, and a closing prayer.”
ask: What is the Liturgy of the Hours? (The Church’s daily prayer.)
What are the two hinges? (Morning Prayer and Evening Prayer.)
What is the main part of each hour? (The psalms.)
practice: Gather students in two choirs facing each other.
Pray a short Morning Prayer: the opening versicle, a hymn (sung or read), Psalm 63 (or another), a short Scripture reading, the Benedictus, intercessions, the Our Father, and a closing prayer.
Alternate verses between the two choirs.
Afterward, share what felt different about praying this way.
script.close: End with the Morning Prayer’s blessing. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray Evening Prayer with your family.”

lessons.saintStory:
Columba, also known as Colm Cille, was born in Ireland in about 521, into a noble family. He studied under holy monks, and he founded several monasteries. He loved books and the psalms, and he spent many hours copying the Bible.
According to an old story, he secretly copied a psalter belonging to another abbot, which led to a quarrel and a battle, in which many men died. Columba was deeply sorry, and as a penance he chose to leave Ireland and not see it again. In 563 he sailed to the island of Iona, off the coast of Scotland, with twelve companions.
On Iona, the monks prayed the psalms at set times of the day and night. From Iona, they carried the faith to Scotland and northern England. Columba died in 597, at the altar. His monastery shows how the Liturgy of the Hours turns the day into prayer.

lessons.title: Devotions
lessons.idea: Popular devotions such as the Rosary, the Stations of the Cross, Eucharistic Adoration, novenas and pilgrimages enrich the liturgy and express the faith of ordinary people.
lessons.question: Which devotion do you know?
lessons.activity: “Stations of the Cross” (30 min). Pray the Stations with images, kneeling or standing at each. Afterwards each student chooses a station and writes what it tells them about Jesus’ love. Read Matthew 14:13–21 for another devotion theme (compassion).
teach: Popular piety includes rosaries, pilgrimages, processions, novenas and veneration of relics (CCC 1674–1676). It should be guided by the liturgy and not replace it (CCC 1675).
The Stations of the Cross follow Jesus’ Passion. The Rosary meditates on the life of Christ with Mary. Adoration is quiet prayer before the Blessed Sacrament.
The Church guards against superstition (CCC 2111). Devotions lead to Christ and the sacraments.
Invite families to share devotions from their cultures.
talk: How do they point to Mass?
quiz: Stations of the Cross have…|Seven|Twelve|Ten|Fourteen stations|3|Tradition.
A novena is…|Nine days of prayer|A feast|A meal|A song|0|Acts 1:14.
The Rosary has…|Five mysteries per set|One|Nine|Fifteen|0|Tradition.
lessons.life: Pray the Stations on a Friday in Lent.
lessons.saint: Leonard of Port Maurice: a friar who spread the Stations of the Cross.
lessons.mem: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Matthew 11:28)
lessons.hook: Show photos or objects: a rosary, a Station image, a pilgrim’s shell, a novena card. “These are ways Catholics pray outside Mass.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name two devotions, their purpose and one way to practice.

script.open: Show a picture of a pilgrim path or a hiking trail. Ask, “Why do people walk to holy places? What do they learn on the way? We are going to take a walk, in prayer, along the way Jesus walked.”
teach: Say: “Besides the liturgy, there are popular devotions. These are prayers and practices, such as the Rosary, the Stations of the Cross, Eucharistic Adoration, novenas (nine days of prayer), pilgrimages, processions and the veneration of saints. They are not required, but they help us to pray and express our faith in ways that fit our culture. They flow from the liturgy and lead back to it.”

Say: “The Stations of the Cross started with pilgrims in Jerusalem who walked the Via Dolorosa, the way of sorrow, to follow Jesus’ steps to Calvary. When it became hard to travel, Christians in Europe set up stations in their own churches. There are fourteen: Jesus is condemned; takes up the cross; falls the first time; meets his mother; Simon helps him; Veronica wipes his face; he falls a second time; meets the women of Jerusalem; falls a third time; is stripped; is nailed to the cross; dies; is taken down; is laid in the tomb. Some add a fifteenth: the Resurrection.”

Say: “At each station we say, ‘We adore you, O Christ, and we praise you, because by your holy cross you have redeemed the world.’ We think about Jesus’ love and what he suffered for us. We also see our own crosses. In Matthew 14:13-21, Jesus fed the crowd, and his compassion is the same as on the way to Calvary. The Stations are prayed especially on Fridays of Lent. Eucharistic Adoration is prayer before the Blessed Sacrament, where we simply remain with Jesus.”
ask: What is a devotion? (A popular prayer or practice that supports our faith.)
How many Stations are there? (Fourteen.)
What do we say at each station? (We adore you, O Christ, and we praise you…)
practice: Set up the fourteen Stations around the room with images.
Walk from station to station together, kneeling or standing, silent, reading each station’s title and a short prayer.
At each, say, “We adore you, O Christ…” and the response.
At the end, sit in silence and write one thing you thought about.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, we thank you for your Cross.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray the Stations with your family during Lent.”

tryit: Pray the Stations of the Cross.
lessons.saintStory:
Leonard was born in 1676 in the town of Porto Maurizio on the Italian coast. He joined the Franciscans and became a preacher. For many years he traveled through Italy, preaching missions: weeks of sermons, confession, and prayer in towns and villages. Huge crowds came, and many people changed their lives.
Leonard loved the Stations of the Cross, a prayer in which we walk with Jesus along the path to Calvary. He set them up in more than 570 places. In 1750, the Pope asked him to put the Stations in the Colosseum in Rome, where many early Christians died for their faith.
He died in 1751, and is the patron of parish missions. Leonard shows how popular devotions like the Stations help us live the faith, and how they come from the liturgy.

lessons.title: Prayer in daily life
lessons.idea: We are called to pray at all times, not only at set times. Offer your work, play and troubles to God in a Morning Offering, short prayers during the day, grace before meals, and an evening review.
lessons.question: How can you pray at school?
lessons.activity: “Daily prayer plan” (25 min). Students build a day plan with a morning offering, a mealtime grace, a short prayer for tests or games, and an evening examen. Practice each. Choose one new habit and a reminder to support it. Read 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18.
teach: Paul urges, “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17). The Church teaches that prayer is possible always (CCC 2697–2698, 2742–2745).
The Morning Offering gives the day to God. Mealtime grace gives thanks. An evening examen reviews the day (CCC 2658–2660).
Short “aspirations” like the Jesus Prayer keep the heart turned to God (CCC 2666–2668).
Help students handle distraction and dryness with patience (CCC 2729–2733).
talk: How can you pray at school?
quiz: “Pray without ceasing” is from…|Genesis|Mark|Exodus|1 Thessalonians|3|1 Thess 5:17.
A morning offering gives God…|Our day|Our time off|Our homework|Our toys|0|Tradition.
Examen is…|A game|A test|A review of the day with God|A chore|2|Ignatius.
lessons.life: Make a prayer card for school.
lessons.saint: Charles de Foucauld: a former soldier who lived a hidden life of prayer in the desert.
misc: “I must find a perfect quiet place to pray.”
lessons.mem: “Rejoice always, pray constantly, give thanks in all circumstances.” (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What can you do while walking, waiting or washing dishes?” Introduce short prayers: Jesus, I trust in you.
lessons.assess: Ask each student to share their prayer plan for one day.

script.open: Set up two clocks. Ask, “How many minutes of the day do you spend praying? How many could you? Think of the day: waking up, walking to school, lunch, homework, evening. Where could God fit?”
teach: Read 1 Thessalonians 5:16-18. Say: “‘Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.’ How can we pray without ceasing? The Church teaches that we can’t be on our knees all the time, but we can make our whole life a prayer. We can offer everything we do to God.”

Say: “Here are some ways. First, a Morning Offering: when we wake, we offer the day to God: ‘O Jesus, through the Immaculate Heart of Mary, I offer you my prayers, works, joys and sufferings of this day.’ Second, short prayers during the day: ‘Jesus, I trust in you,’ ‘Come, Holy Spirit,’ ‘Thank you, Lord,’ or the Jesus Prayer. We can say them while walking, waiting or working. Third, grace before and after meals. Fourth, an evening review: we thank God for the day, say sorry for our failings, and ask for help for tomorrow. Also: reading Scripture, praying the Rosary, going to Mass.”

Say: “Why does it matter? Prayer is a relationship. A friendship needs regular time together. Without it, it fades. With it, it grows. Prayer in daily life helps us stay close to God, face challenges, and remember that God is with us. And if we miss a day or forget, we can start again. God is patient.”
ask: What is the Morning Offering? (A prayer offering the day to God.)
What are some short prayers during the day? (Jesus, I trust in you; Come, Holy Spirit.)
Why pray in daily life? (To stay close to God in a friendship.)
practice: Give each student a plan sheet divided into morning, mealtime, school, afternoon, evening, bedtime.
In each part, write a short prayer: Morning Offering; Grace before meals; “Come, Holy Spirit” before homework; “Jesus, I trust in you” when worried; Examen at night.
Add one new habit you will start this week.
Share your plan with a partner, and pray the Morning Offering together.
script.close: Pray the Morning Offering together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Use your plan every day for a week.”

tryit: Add a morning offering, a mealtime prayer and a bedtime prayer.
Add short prayers for hard moments.
lessons.saintStory:
Charles de Foucauld was born in 1858 in France. He became a soldier and an explorer, and for a time he lived without faith. In 1886, in a church in Paris, he knelt before a priest and made a confession. He later wrote, “As soon as I believed that there was a God, I understood that I could not do otherwise than live for him alone.”
Charles became a Trappist monk, then lived as a servant in Nazareth, a quiet life of prayer and work. After being ordained a priest, he went to live in the Algerian Sahara among the Tuareg people. He built a small hermitage, spent hours in adoration, and made friends with his neighbors. He wanted to bring the Gospel by his presence, kindness and prayer.
In 1916 he was killed by a raiding party. He was named a saint in 2022. Charles shows that we can pray in any place, and offer all of our day to God.

units.title: Praying the Our Father
units.eq: What do we ask when we pray the prayer Jesus gave us?

lessons.title: Our Father: hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come
lessons.idea: We begin by calling God Father and by asking that his name be honored and his kingdom come. The first requests are for God’s glory before our own needs.
lessons.question: Why do we ask for God’s name and kingdom first?
lessons.activity: Illustrate “hallowed be thy name” and “thy kingdom come” with a picture of someone honoring God’s name and a picture of a place where God’s kingdom is growing.
teach: “Our Father” calls God by the name Jesus used (Abba). We pray as his children, and we pray with and for everyone because it says “our” (CCC 2779–2793).
“Hallowed be thy name” asks that God’s name be kept holy by us (CCC 2807–2815). We honor his name by how we speak and live.
“Thy kingdom come” asks for Christ’s reign to grow in hearts and to come in glory at the end (CCC 2816–2821). Lived out: be loving where you are.
Help children see these first requests change our hearts.
talk: Why does Jesus teach us to say “Our” and not “My”?
How can we hallow God’s name at school?
Where do you see God’s kingdom growing?
quiz: The first three requests in the Our Father are about…|Food|God|School|Friends|1|CCC 2803.
“Hallowed” means…|Holy|Hungry|Hollow|Hidden|0|CCC 2807.
We say “Our” because we pray…|With and for everyone|Only for friends|Only for family|Alone|0|CCC 2792.
lessons.life: Say the Our Father each morning slowly, stopping at “thy kingdom come” to name one way you can help it come.
lessons.saint: Francis of Assisi: he wrote his own meditation on the Our Father.
misc: “The Our Father is a list of wishes.”
lessons.mem: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come.
lessons.hook: Say the names of three people you love and watch the children’s faces. Ask: “How do you treat the name of someone you love?” Then introduce God’s name.
lessons.assess: Ask children to explain the first two requests in their own words.

script.open: Ask the students to say the Our Father out loud, quickly. Then say, “Now let’s try something. We’ll say only the first three lines, as slowly as we can, and think about each word.”
teach: Read Matthew 6:9-10. Say: “Jesus taught us to pray: ‘Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come, thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.’ Notice: before we ask for anything for ourselves, we first honor God. The first three petitions are about God’s glory.”

Say: “‘Our Father.’ In Romans 8:15, Paul writes, ‘You have received the spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.’ We call God Father because Jesus invites us to share in his relationship with the Father. We say ‘Our’ because we are not alone: we pray as part of a family. ‘Who art in heaven’ doesn’t mean far away. It means God is above all and everywhere, and also that our true home is with him. ‘Hallowed be thy name’ means ‘may your name be made holy.’ God’s name is already holy. We ask that it be honored in us and by all people.”

Say: “‘Thy kingdom come’ means that we ask for the reign of God to spread, in our hearts and in the world, until Christ comes again. It’s the kingdom of justice, peace and love. This isn’t just waiting: we help build it by what we do. It also asks for the final coming of Christ. ‘Come, Lord Jesus.’ We begin with God’s name and God’s kingdom. When we put God first, everything else falls into place.”
ask: Why do we say ‘Our’ Father? (We pray together as a family.)
What does ‘hallowed be thy name’ ask? (That God’s name be honored and treated as holy.)
What does ‘thy kingdom come’ ask? (That God’s reign of love spread, and Christ return.)
practice: Fold a paper in half.
On one side, write “Hallowed be thy name” and draw a picture of someone honoring God’s name: for instance, someone praying quietly, or a person saying grace.
On the other, write “Thy kingdom come” and draw a picture of the world as God’s kingdom: peace, sharing, kindness.
Pray the first three petitions slowly, one at a time, with a pause after each.
script.close: Pray the whole Our Father slowly. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray the first three petitions every morning.”

lessons.saintStory:
Francis of Assisi loved the Our Father. He is said to have prayed it often. He also wrote a prayer called the Paraphrase of the Our Father, in which he went through each line and added words of praise, so that “Our Father” became “Most holy Father, our Creator, Redeemer, Consoler and Savior.”
When he wrote about “hallowed be thy name,” he asked that “the knowledge of you may be made clearer in us.” For “thy kingdom come” he wrote, “that you may reign in us through grace and bring us to your kingdom, where we will see you clearly.” He prayed with great love for God’s glory.
Francis’s example shows that the first part of the Our Father is about God’s honor before our needs, and that praying it slowly, with love, can open our eyes.

lessons.title: Thy will be done; give us this day our daily bread
lessons.idea: We ask that God’s will be done on earth as in heaven, and then ask for what we need today. We trust that the Father gives us enough and we share it with others.
lessons.question: What do we ask for in daily bread?
lessons.activity: Make a “daily bread” collage: things we need each day, and one thing we can do to share bread with someone who has none. Add a loaf of bread as a sign of the Eucharist.
teach: “Thy will be done” asks to love what God wants, as Jesus did in Gethsemane (Luke 22:42; CCC 2822–2827). God’s will is that all be saved.
“Give us this day our daily bread” asks for what we need and teaches trust (CCC 2828–2831). The word “our” means we ask for everyone and share with the poor (CCC 2830).
The bread is also the Word of God and the Eucharist (CCC 2835–2837). Jesus said, “I am the bread of life.”
Avoid making prayer sound like a vending machine. Trust is the heart.
talk: Why is it hard to say “thy will be done”?
What does it mean to ask only for today’s bread?
How can you help a family who needs daily bread?
quiz: “Daily bread” stands for…|Money|What we need and the Eucharist|Only a sandwich|A treat|1|CCC 2835.
Who prayed “not my will but yours” in the garden?|Peter|Jesus|David|Moses|1|Luke 22:42.
We say “give us” because we pray for…|Only family|Everyone|Only me|No one|1|CCC 2830.
lessons.life: Give thanks before each meal this week, and share some food or time with someone in need.
lessons.saint: Paulinus of Nola: a rich man who gave everything away so the hungry could have bread.
misc: “If I pray for bread, it falls from the sky.”
lessons.mem: Give us this day our daily bread.
lessons.hook: Break a loaf of bread and share it. Ask: “What would happen if no one had any today?”
lessons.assess: Ask children to say what each request means and one way to share bread.

script.open: Hold up a loaf of bread. Ask, “Why do we pray for ‘daily’ bread and not ‘a year’s worth’ of bread? Think about the story of manna in the desert: the Israelites could gather only what they needed each day.” Let students speculate.
teach: Read Matthew 6:10-11. Say: “‘Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread.’ In heaven the angels do God’s will perfectly. We ask that it be done on earth too, and in us. This is not resignation. It means we ask God to teach us to want what he wants. Jesus prayed this way in Gethsemane: ‘Not my will, but yours be done.’”

Say: “Then we ask for our daily bread. This means what we need to live: food, clothing, shelter, health, work. It reminds us that everything comes from God. We ask for ‘our’ bread, not just ‘my’ bread, which includes the hungry. We ask for ‘daily’ bread, meaning enough for today, trusting God for tomorrow. It teaches us to rely on God, and to share. If we have more than we need, we have a responsibility to the one who has less.”

Read John 6:35: “I am the bread of life.” Say: “There’s another meaning too. Jesus is the bread of life. The Church Fathers saw ‘daily bread’ as also the Eucharist, which feeds our soul. So we ask for what we need in body and soul. We also work: Jesus told us to ask for bread, but we also do our part to earn it and to help others. And at Mass, we pray this prayer just before we receive Communion.”
ask: What do we ask for when we say ‘Thy will be done’? (That God’s will be done in us and everywhere.)
What does ‘daily bread’ mean? (What we need for today, in body and soul.)
Why do we say ‘our’ bread? (We pray for everyone, especially the hungry.)
practice: On a sheet of poster board, make a “daily bread” collage with magazine pictures or drawings of things we need each day: food, water, a home, family, health, school, friends.
In the middle, draw bread.
Around the edge, write one action to share your bread with someone in need.
Present your collage to a partner.
script.close: Pray the third and fourth petitions together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Give something to someone who needs it this week.”

tryit: Show what we need each day.
Add one thing you can share.
lessons.saintStory:
Paulinus was born around 354 in what is now France, to a rich Roman family. He was educated, became a senator, and later governor. He married a wealthy Spanish woman named Therasia. They were baptized, and gradually they decided to give up their wealth and live a simple life.
They sold their lands and gave the money to the poor. They moved to Nola, near Naples in Italy, where Paulinus became a priest and later bishop. He built a church for pilgrims and a hostel for the poor, and he wrote letters and poems. An old story says that when a poor widow came, whose son was being held in slavery, and he had nothing left to give, Paulinus offered to take the boy’s place as a slave.
He died in 431. Paulinus lived the Our Father’s prayer for daily bread by sharing what he had.

lessons.title: Forgive us; lead us not into temptation; deliver us from evil
lessons.idea: We ask God to forgive us as we forgive others, to keep us from temptation and to rescue us from evil. The Our Father ends in trust that the Father protects us.
lessons.question: Why must we forgive in order to be forgiven?
lessons.activity: Role-play a time someone says sorry and the other forgives. Draw a shield for “deliver us from evil” and write the names of those who help protect us.
teach: “Forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us” asks mercy for ourselves and gives us the duty to forgive (CCC 2838–2845). Jesus says, “If you do not forgive others, neither will your Father forgive you.”
“Lead us not into temptation” asks that God not let us be led into sin and that he give strength (CCC 2846–2849). God never tempts anyone (James 1:13). He helps us choose well.
“Deliver us from evil” asks God to rescue us from the Evil One (CCC 2850–2854). The last words, “For the kingdom, the power and the glory are yours,” are a doxology added at Mass (CCC 2855).
Be gentle with children who are hurt. Forgiving does not mean staying with someone who is unsafe.
talk: Why is it hard to forgive?
What helps you when you are tempted?
Who helps protect you from evil?
quiz: Does God tempt us to sin?|Only on Sunday|No, he helps us resist|Yes, to test us|Sometimes|1|James 1:13.
We ask forgiveness “as we forgive” because…|Our mercy shows our hearts are open|God needs help|It is easy|It is a rule with no reason|0|CCC 2843.
The last request is for…|A trip|Good grades|A prize|Deliverance from evil|3|CCC 2850.
lessons.life: Forgive someone this week, or ask forgiveness, and pray the whole Our Father at bedtime.
lessons.saint: John Gualbert: a nobleman who forgave his brother’s killer and became a monk.
misc: “God leads people into sin to test them.”
lessons.mem: Forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us; and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
lessons.hook: Tell a short story about two children who fight over a toy. Ask: “What would make it right?”
lessons.assess: Ask children to name the last three requests and say what each asks.

script.open: Ask, “Is it harder to say sorry or to forgive? Why?” Let students discuss in pairs. “Jesus put these two together in one prayer.”
teach: Read Matthew 6:12-15. Say: “‘And forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us.’ After the Our Father, Jesus explained one line: ‘If you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you; but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.’ That is serious. We can’t receive God’s mercy while refusing to give it. It’s not a deal: it’s that our hearts must be open.”

Say: “Forgiving doesn’t mean pretending it didn’t hurt. It doesn’t mean there are no consequences. It means choosing not to hold it against the person, to let go of the desire for revenge, and to wish them well. It’s hard, and sometimes it takes time and prayer. Jesus helps us do it. He forgave from the cross: ‘Father, forgive them.’”

Say: “‘And lead us not into temptation.’ God doesn’t tempt us (James 1:13). We ask: ‘Don’t let us enter into temptation; keep us from giving in.’ Jesus said, ‘Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation.’ (Matthew 26:41) ‘But deliver us from evil.’ We ask God to rescue us from the evil one, Satan, and from all evil. The Our Father ends with trust: Our Father protects us. At Mass we add: ‘Deliver us, Lord, from every evil, graciously grant peace in our days…’ and then the doxology: ‘For the kingdom, the power and the glory are yours.’”
ask: Why must we forgive? (Jesus said God forgives us as we forgive others.)
Does forgiving mean pretending nothing happened? (No; it means letting go of revenge and wishing them well.)
What do we ask in ‘deliver us from evil’? (To be rescued from the evil one and all evil.)
practice: Role-play a situation: one student takes another’s pencil. The other says it hurt. The first apologizes. The second says, “I forgive you.” Practice with different scenarios.
Talk about how it feels to be forgiven and to forgive.
Draw a shield and write on it: “Deliver us from evil.” Around it, write the things you want protection from.
Pray the last three petitions together.
script.close: Pray the whole Our Father with the doxology: “For the kingdom, the power and the glory are yours, now and forever.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Forgive someone this week.”

tryit: Draw a shield for “deliver us from evil.”
lessons.saintStory:
John Gualbert was born around 985, in Florence, Italy, to a noble family. When his brother Hugh was killed in a quarrel, his father told John that he must take revenge.
One Good Friday, John was riding into Florence with armed men when he met the killer, alone on a narrow path, with no place to run. The man dropped to his knees with his arms stretched out in the shape of a cross, and begged for mercy in the name of Jesus, who died on Good Friday. John thought of Christ forgiving from the cross. He put away his sword, raised the man up and embraced him.
He went into a church nearby to pray, and, according to the story, the figure of Christ on the crucifix bowed its head to him. John became a monk and founded a new community at Vallombrosa. He died in 1073. John’s story is the Our Father in action: “Forgive us as we forgive.”
